catalog.description: Every Swarm agent's chat has a pink brain in its title strip, left of the menu. It opens the agent's memory in a panel pinned on the right: a file picker with MEMORY.md first and then each of the agent's facts by title, and the app's markdown editor (edit and preview, with the hint sheet). Save writes a backup of the file's previous text into the app's state folder first, then writes the edit and keeps the fact store in step (the fact's title and scope follow the edit, and the generated index block of MEMORY.md is rebuilt). Undo drops unsaved edits, or with none puts back the version before the last save; the earlier versions list restores any kept version, and a restore keeps the text it replaces too, so nothing is lost. The agent reads the edited text the next time it wakes.
examples: fix a wrong fact an agent learned by editing its text and saving
undo a save that broke an agent's MEMORY.md
how_to: open an agent's chat
click the pink brain at the top right of the chat's title strip
pick MEMORY.md or a fact, edit it, and press save
press undo to put the previous version back, or pick an earlier version from the list

examples: Keep every agent in view while you work in one of them.
Glance at the stats bar to see how many agents are working or waiting to be read and how many tokens are flowing, without opening anything.
Hide studio while you work on this computer, then switch it back on to see everything again.
how_to: Every session is listed, grouped, with its light, name and folder.
Click a row to open it; use the three dots or a right click for its actions; F2 renames it; drag it, or press alt and an arrow, to move it; search at the top.

A row's menu shows each item's key at the right end, and pressing it while the menu is open runs that item, with the same letters as every other menu: r rename, n new session in the folder, c colour, b load blueprint; any other item takes the first free letter of its name, never d or v, which stay delete and archive.

A project heading's three dots lead with new agent, which opens the same select-provider picker every other launch uses, then starts the agent in that project once you choose one; a row's add to files it into a group or a Layout, and a group's or Layout's add pulls agents in.
Show path, in a session row's menu or a project heading's menu, opens a small popup with that session's working folder (or the project folder) in full, with a copy button.
Drag its right edge to resize it; it docks beside the page on a wide screen.
A row shows small icons for what it has: agents running, background shells open, and live timers; hover one for the count and detail. Turn any of the three on or off per density in settings.

A sleeping session wears a sleep icon, an archived one an archive icon, and an inactive project a dashed folder icon after its name; hover one for its name. The show archived tick in the view menu lists every archived session and every inactive project.

When a session's Claude Code is out of date, its three-dot menu turns green: click it for update and restart on top, or shift-click the icon to jump straight to the restart confirm. It is disabled, with a reason, while the session has a running sub-agent, an open shell or a live timer.

When a session's transcript shows an MCP server dropped (an app restart drops them all until reconnected), its three-dot menu turns into a yellow exclamation; hover it for the servers, and pick reconnect mcp (key z) to type the reconnect into the session. It only works while the session is idle and is refused while it is busy. A drop shows after the session's next transcript write, since an idle session writes nothing.
A small pulsing blue workflow mark beside a row's provider icon means that session has a Workflow run going right now; it clears when the run finishes.

SysOp sits at the very top of the list, each company's agent first under its company heading and each project's agent first in its project, marked by a rank insignia (one chevron for a project leader, two for a company leader, a star for SysOp). Rename a leader with F2 or its row menu; closing, deleting or turning one off asks you to type its exact name first.

Cozy shows each agent as a meter: the first line ends in the row's controls with no figure at its right (the thin bar along the row's bottom edge is the context readout), then a second line with its model and, only while something runs, live work as counts (agents running of launched, shells, the next timer), with the model effort at the right end of that line. Detailed is a triage stack: the state word on the first line, every active flag on its own line loudest first (waiting on your permission, host unreachable, process exited, update ready, context 80% or more), then its live work. Compact is unchanged.

The row detail menu ends in show archived: on, each archived session is listed under its project after the project's other rows, drawn asleep with an archived badge, and the search finds it; waking one restarts it, which brings it back. An archived project is listed under its company too, its heading marked archived. Off, archived sessions stay out of the list and the search. The choice follows you to every device.

Click a sleeping agent and a small wake button appears in the middle of its row with an X at the right to cancel; press wake to wake it, or press the X, Escape or tap elsewhere to leave it asleep. (If you turned on wake a sleeping session straight from a click in settings, the click wakes it with no button.) On a phone the drawer now reaches to a thin strip at the right edge; tap the strip to close it.

Hold shift and click a company, project or other heading to open or close everything underneath it at once; the chevron turns into a double chevron while shift is held. Shift+Enter does the same from the keyboard.

Folds (including the providers panel) and row density are kept separately for the desktop and the phone: on a screen 700 pixels wide or less the drawer is the phone's, and what you fold or pick there does not move the desktop's. Pins and order are shared by every device.

A project has no color until you pick one. Press a project heading's kebab and pick a swatch in its color row to set the project's color, or the crossed swatch at the start of the row to remove it; the swarm list's project header takes it at once.

A small bar between the tabs and the search box shows three counts (active agents, in progress, waiting to be read, from this computer and paired ones) and the token rate: the up arrow is tokens generated, the down arrow is tokens in (fresh, cache write and cache read, split on hover). Click the rate to cycle per second, minute, hour and day; click the small chart to cycle the last hour, 5 hours, day and 7 days (hatched slots were not measured). It says stats off or stats paused when that is the case. On a phone it scrolls away with the search row. Both choices are kept per browser. When the feed cannot be read it says so by name (sign in for stats, stats not on this install, stats not readable) instead of waiting. A longer window folds several minutes into each bar, and hovering a bar names the span it covers. If a paired computer is paused, off or unreachable, a hatched band marks the part of the chart that undercounts, in the danger color when it cannot be reached, and a small square beside the rate shows the same at any width.

The stats bar wears no box and shows no hover tips: the counts sit on the left and the token rate sits flush right, with at most one decimal (4.5M). When the pack holds more than one computer, a wolf and that number (this computer and offline ones included) come first, before the counts.

Untick "show stats" in the view menu to hide the counts and token bar under the tabs; hidden, it is not drawn and does not read the stats feed. On by default, kept separately for the desktop and the phone.
Project, company, group and layout colors are drawn whenever one is set. Pick one from the heading's menu (swatches or any custom color).

The pack section under browsers lists this computer first, then each paired one, as rows that look like the agent rows and follow the drawer's compact, cozy or detailed view: the computer icon, a red wolf on the alpha, a light summing up that computer's agents, the name, then cpu, ram and disk flush right (as percents, then small meters, and in detailed a second line with the model, cores, memory and the reserve in use); click a row to open pack. Its heading folds like the others. The pinned heading shows no status light, folded or not.

Drag a section heading (pinned, layouts, groups, companies, rogue agents, terminals, browsers, pack) to put the sections in any order; on a phone drag from the little icon at the heading's left, and the rest of the heading still scrolls. A focused heading moves one slot with alt plus the up or down arrow. Escape cancels a drag. The order is the same on every device, and a section added later joins at its usual place until you move it.

Every group you made sits under one groups heading, built like layouts: click it to fold all the groups out of the way, and each group keeps its own fold, color and members. Drag a group's heading, or press alt plus the up or down arrow on it, to reorder the groups among themselves; drag the groups heading to move the whole block. While you drag a session row the groups heading stays open so every group is a drop target. Shift+click it to fold or open every group at once.

The view menu (the three bars button) has show open sessions and show sleeping sessions, both ticked by default. Open lists your awake sessions and sleeping lists your asleep ones; they are independent, so untick one to hide that set, and with both unticked no awake or sleeping session shows. Show archived and show closed sessions are unticked by default. All are kept per device, so your phone can differ from your desktop.
Right-click a project, company or group heading for the same menu its three dots open; every menu closes when you click away, and only one is open at a time.
Terminals and browsers always have a heading; empty, each says no terminals open or no browsers open. An agent's own shell lists under terminals with its folder.

A group you made with no sessions in it is not drawn (it also hides when the view's filters leave it no row, such as sleeping members with sleeping hidden), and it returns the moment a session is in it. While you drag a row every group shows so you can drop into an empty one. The group itself stays saved.
The view menu's hide empty sections tick, off by default, also hides the terminals and browsers headings while they hold nothing; a drag still shows them.

Type in the search box and the list becomes two sections: AGENTS (every agent whose name, project or folder holds the text, asleep ones included even when show sleeping is off; a pinned agent is listed once, the match is in the accent, and each row offers open session and look around, with its three dots for the rest) and the top CONVERSATIONS (saved conversation hits, each with read around, go to session or resume, copy link and more). Under the box, similar terms from your saved conversations show from 2 letters: arrow down enters them, left and right move, enter takes one, escape goes back to the box. Enter opens the highlighted result. Starting a drag keeps the text.

In the pack section, click a computer to switch it off: its agents and projects leave the list and its row dims with the name struck through; click it again to bring them back. Every computer starts on, and a phone keeps its own switches.

Right-click a session row (or press shift+f10) and pick join the swarm to make it a swarm agent under its project agent, keeping its conversation: a warning says joining restarts it and stops what it is doing, and ok goes ahead; a project with no project agent first says so plainly, and ok creates the project agent. A member's row shows its little swarm character in place of the status light, in its swarm color, its animation telling its status (working, a question, waiting to be read, asleep and the rest); hover it for the status in words. Leave the swarm, in the same menu, makes it a plain session again.

A session row's menu never offers do not disturb: a swarm member shows leave the swarm in its place and any other session shows join the swarm. Mute on the row means only one thing, no notifications from that session anywhere (pop-ups, phone push, texts and every destination, the swarm's own pushes and texts included); its status light keeps updating.

catalog.description: A one line, plain english label of what each live claude or codex session is working on, so a glance at a terminal head tells you what the session is for. It is made by an ai model you route for it alone (it never borrows your chat default), and it is part of the working-on labels plugin, which is off until you turn it on, refreshed when a turn ends and again while a long turn keeps working, never on a timer at idle. Only a few redacted recent messages leave the computer, and only to the provider you routed it to.
examples: Eight agents are open: the line above each prompt bar reminds you which one was fixing the restart picker and which one was porting the settings screen.
You answered a string of yes and continue prompts, so the last prompt says nothing; the line still names the task and its goal.
Point the summaries at a small local model so they cost nothing, while chat keeps using a larger one, and watch the token readout to see what they use.
how_to: Turn on the working-on labels plugin on the plugins page, then open settings, ai summaries and tick use a different model to give the session summary its own model. Until you do, it sends nothing and says it needs a model.
Open settings, then ai summaries to switch the working on line on or off, set the minimum seconds between calls for one session and the calls per hour cap, and see which route is in use.
Finish a turn in any claude or codex session: the line updates on every open browser within about ten seconds, with no reload.
Click the line (or focus it and press enter) to refresh it now.

Click [hide] at the right end of the line to turn the summary off for every browser and stop its model calls, and use the session working on line switch in settings, ai, summaries to bring it back; while no model is picked the line is a link that opens settings there.
Read what the live label cost (last hour and last 24 hours) in settings, ai summaries, and set its token budget there; when it is spent, summaries pause and the panel says when they resume.

examples: Switch the status lights off, then the terminal ring, one at a time, while watching Activity Monitor, to find which kind of motion costs your browser the most.
Keep the spiral and cursor blink but stop the theme background effect.
how_to: Open settings, pick appearance, then the motion tab. While the animations switch is on, a list of fifteen switches appears under it, one per kind of motion.
Uncheck a kind to stop it at once, no reload; check it again to resume. Everything is checked by default.
The choice is kept in this browser only (local storage), so a test in one window never changes your phone or other windows.

Kinds: status lights, avatar spiral, selected terminal ring, dialog glow, effort badges, drawer bands, sparks and steam, busy pulses, attention cues, swarm characters, pop-ins, transitions, layout moves, theme background effect, terminal cursor blink.

examples: Turn animations off on a laptop on battery or a machine with many terminals open to cut gpu work.
Keep a quiet screen while presenting or screen sharing.
how_to: Open settings from the account menu, pick appearance, then the motion tab.

Turn animations off: the working-status spinners and pulses, the effort shimmer, drawer band pulses, the keep awake steam, dialog edge glows, the swarm characters and panel slide-ins go still, the same static look as the operating system's reduce motion setting, whatever that is set to.
The motion tab lists what stops, why you would turn it off, and a small live example that animates when the switch is on and holds still when it is off.
Turn it back on to play them again. The choice is shared with your other devices; an agent can set it with the preferences_update tool (field animations).
Short fades and slides on menus and buttons stay, because they are cheap and carry meaning.

examples: The Spark and the mini are both unreachable while conversations close: a red badge appears on the bell beside the Carnivore mark in the agents drawer, a card says no summary server reachable, and the panel shows how many summaries are waiting. The alert resolves by itself on the first summary that succeeds.
You already know a server is down: dismiss the alert and it stays quiet until the condition clears, or snooze it for an hour.
You want a Slack message when the save pipeline stops, but no pop-up card: tick save pipeline under the Slack destination and untick it on screen.
how_to: Click the bell beside the Carnivore mark in the agents drawer (or under the claw of the closed drawer's icon rail): open alerts first, errors before warnings, each with its count and first and last seen; resolved alerts of the last 24 hours fold underneath. On a phone with the drawer shut, a coloured dot on the claw says an alert is open; tap the claw, then the bell. Clicking any alert card opens the panel too.
Dismiss, snooze 1h, or clear resolved from the panel; each is a route: POST /api/v1/alerts/{id}/dismiss, POST /api/v1/alerts/{id}/snooze {minutes}, POST /api/v1/alerts/dismiss-resolved.
GET /api/v1/alerts?state=active|all for the list and the badge counts; changes also arrive on /ws/events as app_alert.raised, app_alert.updated and app_alert.resolved.
An alert card can be hidden per type: untick that alert's row in the screen column of the routing matrix. The bell and the panel still list it.

Alerts can also be routed to outside destinations (chat, push, email, sms): tick the alert rows (self check, save pipeline, archive, transcripts, account, phone link) under a destination in the matrix.

catalog.description: One time zone for the whole app. Repeating schedules in the task manager (every day at 09:00, weekdays at 09:00, monthly on the 1st) are read in it. It is new york until you pick another, it is saved on the server so every device and every agent sees the same one, and an agent can read and change it with the preferences tools.
examples: You moved to Paris: pick Europe/Paris and your daily 09:00 stand-up repeat comes due at 09:00 Paris time from its next run on.
A one-time reminder set for Friday 15:00 New York time still fires at that exact moment after you change the zone; only repeating wall times are re-read.
An agent asked to schedule a daily 08:30 check reads the zone with preferences_get (time_zone) so it knows whose 08:30 that is.
how_to: Open settings, general, time zone. Type part of a name (paris, new york, tokyo) in the search box and click the zone in the list; it saves at once.
To go back to new york, pick America/New_York, or have an agent send preferences_update with time_zone null.
Agents: preferences_get returns time_zone (absent means America/New_York); preferences_update with {"time_zone": "Europe/Paris"} changes it. A name this server does not know is refused.

examples: See the red menu bar icon, click it, click the update row, and watch the window go from downloading to restarting.
Turn on update automatically and never see the icon, the row, the notice or the window: the app updates itself when no session is working.
Update studio from this computer without touching it, then switch its auto update on.
how_to: Open settings, general, updates. The block shows the running version and what the updater says.

When the menu bar icon turns red with an up arrow, click it and click the first row, 'update to X: download, install and restart'. A small window shows the download, the check, the install and the restart. Nothing else to confirm.
The notice in Notification Center carries an update button; clicking the notice itself does the same.
Press check now to look for a new version, and update now when one is waiting. The app downloads it, stops the server and restarts; your sessions keep running.
Turn on update automatically to download new versions in the background and restart into them when no session is working. It is off by default.
To update a paired computer, open the Pack page, Computers, and use update now or the update automatically switch on its row. A computer on an older version shows 'update it by hand once'.

examples: Walk away with the Carnivore window closed; when an agent asks for permission a banner appears and you press Yes or No on it.
Answer a three-question ask one banner at a time; the answers are sent together after the last one.
A plan approval, a folder trust prompt and a Codex approval each appear as a banner with the dialog's own buttons.
Reply to an agent's free-text question straight from the banner, even with the Carnivore window closed; a session's banners group together in Notification Center.
how_to: In the desktop app, open settings, desktop app, and turn on approval banners. Allow Carnivore under macOS Notifications when asked.

When an agent is waiting on you, press a button on its banner. The press answers the dialog the banner showed; if the dialog changed meanwhile, nothing is typed and a 'this question changed' banner opens the app.

A question that takes only a typed reply shows a reply field on its banner: type and send it (2000 characters at most; a longer one is refused and nothing is sent). Multi-select questions open Carnivore instead of offering buttons.
With desktop notifications: asks only turned on in the desktop app settings, the app mirrors only the toasts that ask you something to macOS.

examples: Claude's startup folder-trust prompt (the quick safety check) in a session you are not looking at shows as a card on the questions tab; only your own press answers it. Claude asks a multiple choice question in a session you are not looking at: the questions tab grows in the drawer with a yellow count, and you answer from its card without switching sessions.
A session on your other computer is waiting on a permission dialog: its card carries a host tag and answering it forwards to that computer, where the dialog is checked again before any key is sent.

A restarted session stops on claude's new MCP server approval (or the resume picker, the bypass warning, or a screen nobody has seen before): a read-only card names the session and shows the screen text; clicking it opens the session, and the card goes away once claude starts.

Turn the cross-session mcp gate on or off under settings, sessions and agents, hold cross-session agent actions. It is off by default.
GET /api/v1/approvals for the list; POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/dialog/answer {fingerprint, choice} to answer; the approvals frame on /ws/events says when to re-read.

A startup screen card has no buttons to answer: click it to open the session and answer there. The screen it showed is also written to the session journal (session-journal/journal.log, event startup_prompt_seen).

POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/dialog/answer-all (MCP session_dialog_questions_answer) answers every question of a multi-question ask in one call; the server types the answers in order, re-reading the screen before every key, and stops with a 409 and a named reason if the screen drifts.

catalog.description: An automation is a cron schedule on this computer's clock plus one thing to do, today a report recipe (Scrooge). The Automations page lists them with their next fire time, newest run and an on or off switch; edit, run now and delete sit on each row. Cron also reads the third Tuesday style, written 2#3 in the day-of-week field, and POST /automations/schedule/parse turns a sentence like every third Tuesday at 5 PM into a cron through the connected AI, for confirmation only. The editor checks the cron as you type and shows the next five fires or the reason it is refused (two fires under 15 minutes apart, or never). Under the selected automation, run history shows each run's status, cost and named reason; consecutive skips with the same reason fold into one row that gives the count and dates. A run with a report opens it in place: totals, projects, lever coverage including the levers that could not be measured, and the findings. Every action is an authenticated route, and the page follows the automations and automation_runs push topics instead of polling. A cron agent target runs the installed claude (claude -p) on a schedule in a project folder under a picked login: read only by default, file edits inside the folder as an opt-in, or no permission prompts only after typing a confirming phrase in the app (never settable over MCP), with a spend cap, turn limit and time limit on every run. A finished agent run shows its final text and a continue in a session button that opens a Carnivore session resuming its conversation. The page has three tabs: automations (the list), sessions (projects, the sessions under each, and the automations on each node, with unassigned for the rest, each node showing its next run and last result) and, while the task manager addon is enabled, task manager (the task manager items that carry a schedule, by list, read only). Schedule this on a session or project in the drawer opens the editor already pointed at it. A scheduler pause switch on the page (and in the menu bar tray menu, which also lists the next three runs and the last three results and opens this page) holds every scheduled run as a skipped run with the reason scheduler_paused; run now still works. The page opens simple: an automations tab of tiles and cards, a sessions tab that is a review feed with a quick-view drawer, and an advanced tab that keeps everything above (table, pane, run feed, counters, scheduler log, commands, pause switch) unchanged. A run title and summary are written by code on the server, never by an AI.

Type every third tuesday at 5 pm into the schedule field, check the read-back and the next fires, and create it.

Choose what it does: run a cron agent, pick a project, write the prompt, pick what it may do, then save. Open a finished run's report and press continue in a session to pick the conversation up by hand.

catalog.description: Beast mode (formerly the auto answer plugin, core since #1899) holds every automatic answer and approval in one place. Its grid is in Settings, Advanced, beast mode: one row per kind of prompt, with two check boxes, beast off and beast on. A prompt is handled for you only when the box for the mode you are in now is ticked, so a row can be off in both, on in one or on in both. Out of the box it behaves exactly as before: the four startup screens (our development channels warning, plain folder trust and external imports in your projects' folders, and no on the claude in chrome prompt) are answered in both modes, while claude permission prompts, codex approvals and agent writes over MCP are handled only while Beast Mode is on. Some things always ask you and have no box at all: questions, free text, plan approvals, any other startup screen, and the hard safety gates such as deletes, purges and renames. Beast Mode itself is armed from the account menu, with its confirmation and auto-off, and a coral bolt sits right of the crown in the bottom bar while it is on. Unticking every box stops every automatic answer and approval.
examples: You want folder trust answered only while you are away: untick its beast off box and keep beast on ticked.

You tick agent actions under beast off: the settings ask first, and a dimmed bolt stays in the bottom bar until you untick it, even with beast mode off.

catalog.description: A mod is a Claude Code plugin that changes how Claude Code looks and behaves; it is code that runs with your permissions and is not sandboxed. The Mods page lists every mod Carnivore finds: the ones installed from the catalog, the ones registered in your Claude settings, and the ones sitting in ~/.claude/mods. Each row shows the name, version, a catalog or local tag, and whether the mod is on, off, or on in only some of your Claude settings files (for example on in 1 of 2). The switch registers or unregisters the mod in every settings file; remove sends a local mod's folder to the trash, or uninstalls a catalog mod through the catalog, after one confirm. A missing, unreadable or unwritable settings file, and an unreadable Claude account list, are said on the page and lock the controls instead of failing quietly. Changes take effect in new sessions. Installing a mod from the warez page runs claude code's own checker (claude plugin validate --strict) on a staged copy, shows the events it handles and the calls it makes on a consent sheet with a trust tick (plus a second tick when the security review flagged it or did not run), refuses a blocked review, never updates a mod by itself, and takes it out of every settings file before its folder moves on uninstall.
examples: See that the hand-installed working-on mod is listed as local and on.
Notice that a settings file Carnivore could not write is named on the page, and the switch can be pressed again once it is fixed.
You open a mod on the warez page, read that it spends plan usage on every refresh, and decide not to install it.
A mod whose review is flagged shows two ticks; the install button stays off until you tick both.
how_to: Open the menu tab and choose mods. The line under the title says changes take effect in new sessions.
Use a row's switch to turn a mod on or off in every Claude settings file; a row that reads on in 1 of 2 is on in only some of them, and the switch finishes the job.
Press remove, then remove again in the confirm: a local mod's folder goes to the trash, a catalog mod is uninstalled through the catalog.
Press get more on warez to browse the mods the catalog publishes.

To install one, open the warez page, pick the claude code mod kind chip, open a mod and press install. Read the sheet: the unsandboxed warning, the events and calls the checker found, the claude code version it needs and which settings files it registers in. Tick the trust box (and the second box when it is shown), then install.
A mod never updates itself: update it from the installed list and read the sheet again. A mod whose security review says blocked cannot be installed, and mods cannot be installed over MCP.

catalog.description: A company is a named group of projects, the tier above them (company, then project, then agent). Create, rename and delete companies, nest one company under another (up to four levels), and file any project under one or take it out. A project with no company is orphaned. A project whose folder sits inside another project's folder shows under that project. Deleting a company orphans its projects and moves its child companies up a level, and touches nothing else. Every browser updates live, and agents can read companies through the carnivore MCP server.

Call POST /api/v1/companies with a name and a parent_id to create a company under another; PATCH /api/v1/companies/{id} with parent_id (null for the top level) to move it, or hq_project_id to set its HQ project.

catalog.description: The crate plugin writes a session or a project, its conversations, their side files and Carnivore's own records into one file. An own crate is byte exact and never redacted; it is fully verified before it is kept, recorded as an export (deep search tags each conversation), and copied and verified at an optional second folder. Encryption is optional and standard age v1 to the public keys in the plugin's settings; the private key stays in 1Password. A share crate is separate: secrets starred, images removed, the home folder hidden, never recorded, and it resumes only as a fork. Every build reads every crate version ever written, and python3 -m src.core.crate_format verifies or extracts one offline.
examples: Export a finished project to a crate on /Volumes/Backup before clearing it off this computer.
Move a finished project to another disk with its code, its conversations and its git state (branch, commit and uncommitted changes) in one file.
Send a coworker a share copy of one conversation with its secrets starred.
Verify a two year old crate with python3 -m src.core.crate_format verify, with no Carnivore server running.
Move a project with its review boards: the boards linked to its tasks travel in the same crate.
Bring back a project you deleted from a crate: restore it at its old folders, then wake the sessions you want.
how_to: From a shell or a test, run python3 -m scripts.crate.cli (setup, export, send, restore, verify, undo, cycle) with a bearer token from CARNIVORE_TOKEN or 1Password: it exports on one Mac, moves the crate to another with its sha256 checked, restores it there (refusing, with nothing written, when the plan has blockers) and can verify and undo it. Details in docs/crate.md, section 11.1.

Under "restored" in the crates plugin settings, press undo on a finished restore and confirm: it removes the rows, files, backup points, sessions and project that restore wrote and puts back what it changed. Anything already here or changed since stays and is listed; a later restore of the same source, a running crate job or an interrupted restore blocks it, with nothing written.
Press download on any crate row (recorded, found, or on a project page) and your browser saves the crate file. It is streamed from the crates folder, so a large crate is not loaded into memory.

Press remove on a crate row (recorded or found) in the crates plugin settings or on a project page and confirm: the crate and its checksum file move to the Trash, where you can put them back. A recorded crate stays in the list marked removed; tick the second folder option to take that copy too.
Turn the crates plugin on in the Plugins page; optionally set a second folder and age public keys in its settings.
Open a project on the Projects page and press export this project in its crates group.
Choose own copy or share copy, tick encrypt if you want it, press preview, read the counts and any blocker, then press export.
Tick include the project's files (own copy only) to carry the folder's files too; the preview lists the skipped folders with their sizes.
Read the plugin data rows of the preview: a plugin's review boards of the project's tasks are carried in an own copy; a store whose folder setting is blank is listed with that reason.
Put every session of the project to sleep first: a running session blocks the export.
Press verify on a crate to check every copy again; a pass records when it was verified.

Press restore on a recorded crate, press preview to see which folders it lands in and what blocks it (nothing is written yet), then press restore: the project, its sessions (all asleep), conversation files and records come back, and the done screen has a wake button per session. A crate encrypted with age asks for its private key in the dialog.

Restore a crate that came from another Mac: copy it into the crates folder (or press "open a crate file" and pick it, with its .sha256 file if you have one), press restore on its row under "found in this folder", then preview and restore as for a recorded crate.

Under include backups in the export dialog, tick conversations and any plugin folder listed there (review boards: this project's boards); a folder switched off in the save plugin's backup menu shows greyed. On import, a crate from another computer shows one tick per backup family, on by default.

catalog.description: Deep search is built into the app. It turns the agents drawer's search box (its context mode) into a search of the text of every conversation on this computer, Claude and Codex, read from the live transcripts (what you and the agent said; tool output is not indexed). Results come back one group per conversation: its session name, project and date, how many matches, and its best few hits with the match marked. A small ledger / best hits toggle in the results header picks the layout (remembered per device). The ledger names each conversation (session name, else its first prompt, else its folder), says whether it is live, asleep, never opened here, original deleted or on another computer, and shows two short hits with "N more in this conversation" that loads the rest in place; best hits is a flat list ranked best first with you / agent / tool chips. The picked hit offers read around, go to session or resume, branch here, copy link (a link that reopens that message's context window), bookmark this message and only this conversation; a hit with no session or read from a backup offers read around and copy link only. A conversation Claude Code deleted but the conversation backups hold stays searchable and carries a dashed "from backup" tag (the text is read from the backup itself, nothing is copied; Codex conversations and sub-agent files too), and one that an export bundle holds carries a quiet "exported, in bundle X" tag, and conversations changed since they were indexed are one dim line above the results. What it reads is a setting in settings, under the pipeline tab (what deep search reads): people only (the sessions you typed in), people plus headless sessions, or everything, subagent transcripts included, which is the default; a change takes effect in the background with no restart, and a scope that leaves subagents out is said by name above the results instead of showing a bare zero. The index mirrors your disk file by file: when a transcript file is deleted or moved its rows go at the next pass (unless the save plugin is on and holds it), and a second copy of the same conversation keeps its own. The index is a disposable cache file that rebuilds itself from your transcripts if it is ever deleted, and searches keep answering from the older index until the new one is complete. It is always on. The save plugin adds the backup fallback: with save off the results still show, a deleted conversation is no longer found from backup, and a line says the index is paused. With another computer paired, each computer searches its own transcripts and the results merge: a conversation held by the other computer carries a small tag with that computer's name, one held by both is listed once and says so, and a computer that did not answer is named in one quiet line instead of delaying the rest. A conversation on the other computer opens only when a live session of it is listed here; otherwise its row says which computer holds it. Agents get the same search, peer hits included and tagged, as the conversation_search tool. Reading around opens a context window: the hit centered among the messages around it, more loading as you scroll, with open agent and, for a hit on this computer with a bookmark at or after it, restore bookmark as a clone. Agents get the window through the deepsearch_context_get tool.

examples: Pop a widget, the home page, a dashboard, a Swarm agent chat or a page out of the desktop app and it opens as its own window, listed in the Window menu.
Quit with three pop-outs open, start the app again, and all three come back at their old size and place; one you closed before quitting does not.

Pop a terminal out of the widget menu or a tab menu and its session leaves the main window and opens in a terminal window of its own. Clicking that session in the drawer brings the terminal window forward.
Open two pop-outs, choose Window, Merge All Windows, and they become tabs of one window; Move Tab to New Window pulls one back out. In a browser tab the page shows no title strip at all.

Hide the app with a session scrolling output, then show it: the terminal is already current. With more than 16 terminals open, close a few and the ones that fell back return to the fast renderer when you look at them.
Drag a terminal tab (or a widget header) past the edge of the desktop app window and let go: it opens in a window of its own with the cursor on its title strip, and the terminal keeps running.
how_to: In the desktop app every pop-out button opens a window of its own. Opening the same one again brings the existing window forward.

Choose pop out in a terminal's menu to give a session its own terminal window: the session moves out of the main window, has no drawer or home screen of its own, and shows a short panel (asleep with wake, no longer running with reopen) while it has no live session.
The Window menu lists the open windows and Cmd-backtick cycles through them.
The windows open again after a restart, where they were. A window you closed yourself stays closed.
In a plain browser a pop-out is still a new tab.

Window, Merge All Windows joins windows of the same kind (two pop-outs, say) into one window with a tab bar; Move Tab to New Window splits one out and Show Tab Bar toggles the bar. A pop-out and a terminal window never merge.

Green button or Ctrl-Cmd-F takes a window full screen; Spaces, Mission Control and Stage Manager treat it like any Mac app. The title bar is hidden and the page keeps its top strip clear of the traffic lights; drag that strip to move the window.

A hidden window keeps running, so bringing it back shows it current with no catch-up wait. A terminal that fell back to the plain renderer under load gets its fast renderer back when it is shown and one is free.

Drag a terminal tab or a widget header out past the window edge and release to tear it into its own window at the cursor (Escape cancels). A torn-out terminal leaves the main window's tabs; a widget is copied, as its pop-out is. Closing the torn window leaves the session running. A plain browser does nothing.

catalog.description: For people writing a plugin. Sideload copies a folder holding a plugin manifest (cplug.json) into the host, installs it as local/<name> with the unverified mark, and runs it like any other sidecar. It has its own switch, separate from developer mode, and the switch expires after twelve hours. Turning it off stops and hides every sideloaded plugin; your source folder is never touched.
examples: Try a pixel pet you are building without publishing it: sideload the folder, tick its permissions, watch it run.
Leave the switch on overnight: it turns itself off after twelve hours and the sideloaded plugins stop.
Build a run viewer: pick a run in the slide-out menu and read it full size on the page beside it.
how_to: Turn on developer sideload (it shows twelve hours).
Sideload a folder that holds a plugin manifest (cplug.json); the plugin appears as local/<name> marked unverified, switched off with no permissions.
Turn the switch off to stop and hide every sideloaded plugin; your source folder is never touched.
A sideloaded plugin whose carnivore.json asks for a page gets its own rail key: the slide-out is its menu and the main area shows its page; on a phone a menu | view switch picks one.

catalog.description: The developer widget is a tab strip over a list of monitors. The pipeline tab is the pipeline widget itself: the plugin status squares with the engine's status line (no rebuild button there; rebuild from Settings, pipeline), what is running now and the queue, and the pipeline chart of recent runs (name, area, run time, how long ago, runs); the pipeline tab came back 2026-10-12 on the owner's request, #1689, after the other operator's #1682 U1 removed the old job version. The scheduled tab is a chart in the same look (item 542, #1701): one row per automation with its name, what ran its last run in plain words (schedule, missed run, retry, run now by the owner's name, or run now by an agent's session name), its area (the session it messages, else its project, else machine), how long the last run took, how long ago, and the next run. Over the chart two short sections (2026-10-12): running lists each automation run in progress with what ran it and how long it has run, and queue lists the next scheduled fires soonest first (automations' next runs and, with the task manager plugin on, scheduled task items), at most eight and then "+N more"; both follow the global / sessions / both switch. The figure columns keep the room their widest value needs, so a run time is never cut off. A narrow tab drops the area and then what ran it, never the run time, and a next run a day or more away reads in days and hours (in 6d 23h), so a weekly or monthly schedule is never cut off either. The mark before a name is a shape as well as a color: a filled circle ok, a diamond error, a dash skipped. A global / sessions / both switch on top picks Carnivore's automations (global), the task manager's scheduled task items with their next fire (sessions, read only while the task manager plugin is on; with it off the sessions view says so), or both; the choice is remembered in this browser. Who pressed run now is kept in the run's own notes when the button is pressed (no new column). The scheduled tab updates from the server's pushes (the automations and automation runs topics, and the task manager's list topic), and the pipeline tab from the pipeline topic, with no timed polling while the live connection is up; only the selected tab reads anything, and the chosen tab is remembered in this browser. The selected tab is the lighter fill and the other tabs the darker one. A new monitor is one entry in the widget's monitor list. The sent tab (the owner, 2026-10-14, #1805: "a small flowing list like the others in the dev widget so i can monitor when i send things") is the pipeline tab's layout: a strip on top with a status line ("3 in this browser, 1 not sent") and the copy all and download keys, then "in this browser" (the copies the browser outbox still holds because the server did not answer or refused them, each with retry, copy and, on a refused one, discard keys), then the chart of your recent Task Manager replies, answers, board rounds and adds with where each stands with the agent: waiting to tell, telling in a few seconds, holding while the agent is busy, told with the agent's name and when, read, filed, or not told and why. It updates from the server's pushes with no polling at idle, and with the Task Manager plugin off it still shows the copies kept in this browser. The log tab (the owner, 2026-10-15, #1827: "a log viewer to the dev widget as a new tab, top strip is buttons for each status to filter each type. scrolling not all inclusive") is, since #1861, the one shared log viewer, the same one the logs page (#logs, and the menu bar's Logs... row) shows. It reads records, not lines: a Python traceback or stderr text stays with the event it follows, its line count shows on the row in the danger color and opening the row shows the whole record as JSON with the traceback under it. A strip on top has one toggle for each level (error, warn, info, debug), all on at first and remembered in this browser, one chip per source, the server's log level (changed live, or back to the .env value), export (the records shown, as a .jsonl download) and clear. Under it a text filter (write /pattern/ for a regular expression) and a session filter that matches any of the ways the log names a session. Click a field on a row to show only that value, Alt-click to hide it; each active field filter is a chip you click to remove. The list follows new records at the bottom; scrolling up pauses it and a "N new, jump to live" button brings it back. Load older pages back through the file and its rotated copies. The viewer keeps at most 10,000 records or 8 MB and says when it drops the oldest. Secrets are masked again before anything is shown. It updates from the server's pushes with no polling at idle.
examples: Press run now on an automation and see run now by your name in the ran by column.

If a send shows under in this browser, press retry to send it now, copy to take its text, or discard to drop a refused one; copy all and download take everything.
Press the log tab to read the newest server log lines; press a level to hide or show its lines, your choice is remembered.
Scroll up to read older lines; scroll back to the bottom and the list follows new lines again.

catalog.description: Widget Lab frames the shared widget harness (the page the capture pipeline drives) inside the app. Pick a widget (notes first), a theme and a fixture (data, empty, stress); the page draws the widget in the home grid, the terminal grid, the sidebar area and the pop-out window, marks a host the widget's declaration does not place it in, lists each host's published sizes with the floor, and keeps the widget box at its published size whatever the page width. A json box takes routes laid over the fixture (only parsed, never run, with plain errors); a save made in the widget plays inside the frame and reads back, and goes nowhere else. The frame isolates its own storage, so it never touches the app's real token, and answers every request from the fixture. A capture button on each host card runs the capture pipeline for exactly that state, with the widget's own menu open when asked, and writes a png plus metadata (widget, source revision, host, size, theme, fixture hash, state). A capture that cannot run, finds a problem or has a broken fixture is shown as failed, never as a pass. The harness page now also loads the app's popup stylesheet last, so a widget's menu is drawn on the themed popup surface there as it is in the app.
examples: A scenario of one route, GET /sessions/cloude_billing-api/note with a body of your own text, makes the notes widget show that text in every host.
A scenario route with a typo is reported as never asked for, and a capture of it fails with that reason.
A widget with a hidden 5 second polling timer reads 12 hidden requests a minute and fails; the same check runs over every widget with python3 -m scripts.widgets.idle.
how_to: Turn on developer mode in settings, advanced, open the plugins page from the menu tab, find widget lab and press its switch, then open the widget lab tab.
Pick notes, a theme and a fixture; press the menu open switch on a host card to see the widget's own menu on the popup surface.
Paste a json scenario of routes into the box, press apply, and edit the note: the save reads back inside the frame only.
Press capture or capture with menu on a host card to write a png and its metadata.

Press the idle traffic key on a frame's caption: the lab measures a simulated minute with the widget shown and one hidden, and the word beside the key reads green when a hidden widget sends nothing, coral with the count otherwise.

catalog.description: While the approval inbox has an open question, the sidebar rail grows a questions key below menu and agents: a question mark with the waiting count in yellow, whose glow pulses when a new one arrives. It opens a yellow slide-out over the agents list: a scrollable list of every open question, oldest first so nothing moves when a new one lands at the end. Each question is one cell outlined in the theme of the session it comes from (the session's own pin, its project default, else the global theme), holding the standard question card: one layout for every kind (a startup screen, bash, an edit, a question, a plan, an agent action, a codex approval, an unreadable prompt), with a kind badge and stripe, who and where, how long it has waited and one plain sentence saying what is asked, written from the structured data instead of claude's own text. Cards start open (click a head to fold one to that sentence); each shows its 2 to 4 facts (the folder, the command, what yes and no do, the risk), the raw text folded under details, every option as its own button in screen order in plain words, multi select, your own answer, approve and deny, a footer chip saying whether beast mode would answer it, it always waits for you, it is an mcp write or it is read only, and go to session. A card you fold stays folded while it waits. A session stopped on a startup screen (folder trust, an mcp server, the bypass permissions warning, external imports) shows that screen's warning and its real options, and your click presses exactly that one; nothing answers a startup screen for you, beast mode included. A startup screen whose options cannot be read safely (sign in, a picker, an unknown screen) stays a read only card that says why. Answering resolves the cell and it collapses out; the last answer removes the key and the slide-out closes back to agents. Keys on a focused cell: up and down move, enter opens a folded card, 1 to 9 press that option, enter submits a multi select, escape closes the slide-out. Controls are 44px tall on a phone. Questions from the paired computer show too. The tray icon doors are unchanged.

catalog.description: The flow plugin rebuilds a multi-agent run two ways from one collector. The swimlane flow chart: one lane per agent session with subagents nested under their parent, blocks for the work each did, and arrows for crosstalk messages, spawns, subagent launches and returns, task manager posts and owner replies, every item carrying the ids it came from and an arrow no exact key proves marked inferred; an agent calls flow_get (or the owner its route), and with html set gets one self-contained page to post to the task manager. The flow tab: a live chat of the same run, ordered by cause instead of a time axis, with each agent's words as a bubble in its own color (a subagent stepped in under its parent) and cards between them for tasks, crosstalk, spawns, subagent launches and returns, task manager posts and runs of tool calls (folded, open to see each call). The tab is for testing and stays out of the tab strip until the plugin setting show tab is switched on (it ships off). The tab follows the run as it happens over the push while it is open and does nothing while it is closed. The plugin ships off; finished charts are kept as snapshots in its own flow.db.

catalog.description: One faint pop-out control floats at the top right of the home screen (the desktop home has no top bar since 2026-09-30) and opens a menu: pop out home, wallboard, then every home board. Pop out home opens the home screen alone in its own browser window, titled carnivore stats, with no drawer and a compact bar. The window keeps its numbers live over the same events feed as the main window, opens no terminal and never votes on a pane size, remembers its size and place, re-lays out to whatever size it is dragged to, and has a focus main window link that raises the window that opened it. It uses the sign-in the main window already holds; signed out it says to sign in from the main window. Wallboard opens the same page as a wallboard: only the home analytics widgets, no bar, no handles, read only, sized to fill the window and following the synced home layout live; a board in the menu opens the wallboard for that board. Analytics widgets can also be placed beside terminals in a saved terminal layout.

Put a cost and tokens wallboard on a wall screen while the main window drives the agents.

Leave it open behind other windows; its numbers keep updating, and it catches up by itself after a sleep, a dropped network or a server restart.

If a strip reading offline, data may be stale appears in its bottom left corner, the window has lost its live link for that long: press retry, or reload it. If a pill reading new version available or update ready appears at the top, press reload to run the new install.
Click focus main window to raise the app window that opened it.

Choose wallboard from the same menu to open the home analytics widgets alone in a window for a big screen, or choose a board to open that board's wallboard; changes to the home layout in the main window appear there live.

catalog.description: Keep awake stops a session auto-sleeping and, while any session has it on, holds this computer awake with a caffeinate assertion. The widget shows exactly that state: a count of the sessions kept awake, one line saying whether the computer is held awake (read from mac_awake on GET /auto-sleep, which reports whether the server's caffeinate child is running), and one row per kept-awake session with its status light, its name and, when the widget is wide enough, its project. Each row's cup turns keep awake off through the same route the terminal bar and the drawer use. There is no since-when column because nothing records when keep awake was turned on. The widget is hidden by default, so no saved layout changes; add it from the Widgets list on either page. The drawer also always shows the cup on every kept-awake row, in every density.
examples: Before leaving for the night, check which sessions are still holding the computer awake.
Turn off keep awake on a session you forgot about, without opening it.

catalog.description: A launch profile is a structured record of how an agent starts: the harness (claude, codex or a plain shell), the account it uses (it follows the active one; pinning an account is not available yet), the endpoint (native, or one of your AI connections such as openrouter or lm studio), the model (the harness default, a fixed one, or ask at launch), and the permissions posture. Advanced fields (extra flags, environment variables, secret variables read from the keychain, the shell startup file, a before-launch step) and an expert custom command are folded away. A live preview shows the exact command and environment, with secrets as names and key hints only. The page replaces the wrappers page at the same menu row.
examples: Run claude through openrouter with a model picked from the connection's live list.
Keep a codex launch profile that skips all permission checks, marked clearly in the list.
Add qwen code as a launch profile with its logo; its sessions show that name and logo in the sidebar and tabs, with no status light.
how_to: Press new and pick a template: claude subscription, claude via openrouter, claude via lm studio, codex yolo or plain shell.

Or start a custom agent: pick custom agent (any command you type, with an icon you choose) or one of the ready presets (pi, oh-my-pi, claude code, codex cli, github copilot cli, devin, factory droid, kimi cli, opencode, kilo code, hermes agent, qoder cli, qwen code, letta, cursor cli, mastra code, antigravity cli, grok cli).
Change the fields; the preview shows the exact command as you type.
Press save. Use check to run the harness, duplicate to copy, make default to use it for new sessions of that harness.
Delete asks you to move anything still using the launch profile to another one first.
The icon row shows the chosen icon at 24px beside its id, and the list shows the same 24px icons.

catalog.description: The bar shows the Layout's name and one box with one mode toggle inside it: a magnifying glass in search mode, a ">" in command mode. Search mode (the default) runs the query in every member terminal through that terminal's own search, with the same "in prompt only" switch, a count per terminal and in total, and next and previous across terminals. Command mode sends the typed line plus Enter to every live member whose ">" toggle is on, after showing how many will receive it ("to 2 of 3", a chip that also opens a menu to choose which terminals); a member that is working right now asks first, and a pane stopped on a dialog is refused rather than answered. Each member terminal carries the ">" toggle in its title bar, on by default and stored with the Layout so every device agrees - the bar's recipients menu sets the same value, and a clean send says nothing further (Enter is already the confirmation); a skip or a failure still reports in the result line. While the desktop drawer is collapsed to its mini rail, the box right-justifies to the header's right edge. In command mode a line that starts with "/" or "$" opens a skill list under the box: every global skill plus the project skills that every terminal the line would reach has, filtered as you type, each with its one-line description and scope.
examples: Three agents on one repo: search "error" to see which of them hit a failure, then send "git status" to all three at once.
Leave a long-running session's ">" off so a broadcast "npm test" only reaches the other terminals.
how_to: Type in the box: search mode (the magnifying glass, the default) finds the text in every terminal at once; each terminal shows its own count and the bar shows the total.
Press Enter or Shift+Enter to walk the matches from one terminal into the next; the prompt icon limits the search to prompts you sent, the same switch as a single terminal's search.
Click the mode toggle to switch to command mode: its icon swaps from the magnifying glass to ">".
Turn a terminal's ">" off in its title bar to leave it out, type a command and press Enter: it runs in every live terminal whose ">" is on, with no confirmation beyond the send itself.
Escape clears the box, and a second Escape leaves it.

In command mode, start the line with "/" (Claude Code) or "$" (Codex) to list skills: every global skill plus the project skills each receiving terminal shares. Keep typing to filter, Up and Down to move, Tab or Enter to insert, Escape to close, or click a row.

catalog.description: Edit layout arranges the screen you are on, the home screen or a session's terminal page, on a desktop window. Its one entry is the edit layout item of the account menu, which the account chip at the bottom left of the agents drawer opens. While it is on, every widget is outlined with a remove control and an arrow beside its top left icon that opens the widget's actions (hide or remove, extend down or pull back a row, and settings for a widget whose copies keep their own), the splitters between widgets are drawn so they can be dragged, and a widget drawer lists every widget as a tree by type (or one list by name, kept per device) with each widget's icon, a fuzzy find box and a kind select beside it, and the analytics charts as a family that folds open. Any widget drops anywhere: onto the screen exactly where you let go, into the sidebar's widget area or its glance area; press a row to add it where it is designed to go. A box a widget was not tested for draws a generic icon and "not available at this size" instead of the widget. A widget switched off on the widgets page is never added: pressing or dropping it, or dragging a splitter past a widget's smallest size, shows one short line saying why. Every change is final the moment it is made: there is no undo, reset or cancel, and the one button, done, or Escape just leaves the mode. A removed widget stays in the drawer and drags back with its settings. Every change is saved the way that screen already saves: the home screen on this browser, a session's terminal page synced to every device. Below 1024 wide there is no edit layout; the widgets menu stays the phone's show and hide.
examples: Put the notes widget in a row of its own at the top of the home screen by dragging it there.
Take the masthead off the home screen to give the session lists more room, and bring it back later from the widget drawer.
Make a rearrangement and press Escape: it is already saved, and the mode closes.
On a session's terminal page, turn on show what can't go here to learn that projects fits only home and the pop-out.
A game plugin declares medium and large in its cplug.json fits: its widget offers exactly those two in the size gear and refuses to shrink below its declared smallest size.
how_to: Open the agents drawer, press the account chip at its bottom left, and choose edit layout.
The widget drawer opens as the edit layout tab in the left sidebar; switch to another tab and back without leaving edit layout, and press the tab's close key to finish (it keeps the edit).

Find a widget in the widget drawer: by default a tree with one fold per type (kpi, list, monitor, feed, tool, chart) and its widgets sorted by name; press the list button in the drawer's title row for one flat list by name. Each row leads with the widget's icon, the same one on the widget's top left corner on the home screen, and a small settings mark after the name means the widget has configurable views or settings. Type in the find box for a fuzzy search (the letters in order, best match first, matched letters highlighted); the folds open while you search and come back as you left them. Shift+press a type to fold or open every type. Pick a kind in the select beside the find box to narrow it. Drag a row onto the screen, or press it to add it at its designed place.

Press the (i) on a row to open the widget's description card: what it shows, a preview, its suggested sizes, where it can go, its options and who made it. The widgets page opens the same card in its detail pane.
In a dashboard pop-out, press add widgets in its top bar: the same widget drawer opens over the window, and what you add is saved to that dashboard only.
On the terminal page, drag or press the session, terminal or browser card to pick one of your live ones from a list and add it the same way.
Press arrange layout, in the components list, to open edit mode and rearrange by hand.
Press the small arrow beside a widget's top left icon to list what that widget can do; outside edit layout the same menu opens from the icon itself.
Press a widget's remove control to take it off; drag the splitters to resize.
Press done or Escape to leave; every change was saved when you made it. Drag a removed widget from the drawer to put it back.
Press done, or the layout button again, to keep it.
Drag a widget's side edge to resize it: a widget covering several rows has the full height edge to grab, and its four corners move the side and the row boundary together.
Turn on "show what can't go here" to see why a widget is missing from this screen; press one of its dimmed rows to read the full reason.

A plugin's panel view (a developer-sideloaded plugin that declares the panel surface) is listed in the drawer while the plugin is on; press it to add it. It lands at large, or at its smallest size when it does not offer large, and the cell menu size gear lists only the sizes the view declares.

catalog.description: The pipeline reads your conversations once and feeds its plugins (usage stats and deep search). examples: Open the app on your phone by scanning the link the menu bar hands you.
Hide the menu bar icon in settings, desktop app and keep working from the Dock alone; the Dock menu still lists what is waiting on you.
how_to: Carnivore lives in the Dock: closing the window leaves it running, and a Dock click brings the window back where you left it.
Settings, desktop app, show menu bar icon removes or restores the menu bar icon at once.

Cmd-Q quits the app and shows a one-time notice the first time; the engine keeps running with your agents, phone and web alerts, and the next launch picks it up again without a click. Quit and Stop Engine in the app menu and the menu bar also stops the engine.
If an engine from another version is still running when you open Carnivore, one dialog offers to restart it on this version (your agents keep running) or to quit and leave it.
Click the Carnivore icon: the header says whether the server is running, its version and whether a phone can reach it; Option-click adds a Debug submenu.
When a session is waiting on you, N Need You lists it; a click opens the approvals popup on that session, or the session itself at a startup prompt.
Open Sessions for the waiting and most recent sessions: Open in App, Watch in Terminal (read only), Type in Terminal, Copy Attach Command, or Restart... in the app.

Each session row wears a small status dot (green working, yellow waiting on you, light blue notice, gray idle as a disc and unknown as a ring, dark gray dead, red disconnected); one row per paired computer opens the Pack computers tab.

Phone Access copies the measured address or shows it as a QR, copies the sign-in code and shows the authenticator QR; Keep Mac Awake and Autonomy (Beast Mode, Swarm, Pause Scheduler, Stand Down) sit below it.

Click the Dock tile while the server is down: a small status window shows the same server-stopped facts and the Start Server, Terminal (Offline), Open Server Log in Console and Copy Diagnostics buttons; with the server up it raises or opens the app window.

While the server is down the header counts the agents still alive in tmux; Start Server, Terminal (Offline)..., Open Server Log in Console and Copy Diagnostics come first, and Server & Troubleshoot holds Start in Debug Mode, Kill Port Holder... and Reinstall Server Environment....

Set a feed with the CARNIVORE_UPDATE_FEED_URL environment variable or updates.feed_url in config.json; the menu then checks for updates at launch and a few times a day, downloads in the background and offers Restart to Update.
Server & Troubleshoot, Uninstall, Uninstall Carnivore... removes the app, its settings and its keychain items after you type UNINSTALL; your projects folder and Claude Code and Codex logins stay.
The Dock icon shows a red number when sessions are waiting on you, the same count as the menu bar icon's Need You row.
Right-click or hold the Dock icon for New Session, Recent Projects and the sessions waiting on you.
The Dock icon hops once when a new question arrives while Carnivore is behind other windows.
The menu bar at the top of the screen has Carnivore, File, Edit, View, Session, Window and Help; Help has the macOS search field, and Carnivore Help opens the help page in your browser.
File has New Session, New Window and Open Project; Session has Restart, Stop, Rename and Answer Waiting Question, which act on the session you are looking at.
Settings, desktop app, option key as meta makes Option-B, Option-F and Option-Backspace move and delete by word in every open terminal, with no reload.
Help, Export Diagnostics... (also in the menu bar icon menu) saves a redacted diagnostics zip wherever you choose; crash dumps and crash lines stay on your computer and nothing is sent.

Session menu, Open In Terminal App... (or the terminal widget menu, open in terminal app) opens the session in the terminal app you picked in settings, desktop app: Ghostty, iTerm2, Terminal, Kitty, WezTerm, or a custom command that Carnivore shows you in full and asks you to confirm the first time and whenever it changes.
Drag a folder from Finder onto the Carnivore icon in the Dock: it opens that project, or asks to add the folder as a project first.
Drag a file or folder from Finder onto a terminal: its quoted full path is typed at the prompt (not sent), so the agent can read it.

Session menu, Reveal in Finder and Open in Editor (and File menu, Reveal Project in Finder and Open Project in Editor) open the folder of the session in view or its project; the editor is the default editor set in Settings, General.

catalog.description: The MCP server monitor is a catalog plugin (carnivore/mcphealth, sandboxed): it is no longer built into the app, so install it from warez and approve what it asks for. An install that had the built-in copy on keeps its settings, stays off until you approve the new sheet, and gets one alert pointing at warez. Until installed and on: with it off nothing is measured, no server is probed, no client log is read and no row shows the yellow !. Turned on it works as before: for every live Claude Code and Codex session it reads the configured servers, the session's own MCP client log, the stdio processes and a 60 second reachability probe, and names each down server with its reason in the row's tooltip. Its settings choose which servers may raise the !: all of them, only the ones you list, or all but the ones you list. A server left out is still measured but never shows on the row and never notifies. With notifications on, a server that may warn sends one notification when it goes down in a session and one when it comes back, never repeated while it stays down and none in the first minute after Carnivore starts.
examples: A remote server you know is often offline keeps lighting the !; you put it on the block list and the row stays quiet while every other server still warns.
You only care about the carnivore server: you choose only the listed servers and list carnivore.
You turn notifications on and your phone hears once when the memory server drops in a session, and once when it is back.
how_to: Open warez from the menu tab, install mcp health, then open the plugins page and press its switch; it asks to read which mcp servers your sessions have and to raise a notice.
In its side pane pick which servers may raise the !: all servers, only the listed servers, or all but the listed servers, and type the server names separated by commas.
Tick send notifications to get one notification when a server goes down in a session and one when it comes back; mute the type mcp server down or back in the notification settings.

catalog.description: Carnivore connects to a messaging provider (the imsg bridge, speaking the Carnivore Provider Protocol) and binds sessions to conversations, in, out or both. A text from you reaches the bound session: a threaded reply goes to the session that sent the original, a leading @name to that session, otherwise the default one; with several bound and none named, Carnivore texts back which session. Only your own handles, as imessage, are accepted; an sms gets a short reply asking for imessage, and a stranger gets nothing. While a permission, question or startup dialog is open the text is held and you get one text saying so; it goes in when the dialog closes, and several held texts arrive as one batch, oldest first, each dated. An asleep session is woken. An edit or unsend replaces or drops a held text, and sends a short note after delivery. A bound session sends with messaging_send: text only, secrets starred, rate limited, and logged first. Secrets live in the keychain only, and the provider's address is write-only.
examples: You text restart the feed while the session is asking a permission question; you get held for trader, and the text goes in after you answer the dialog.
Three texts sent while the computer was asleep arrive as one message, oldest first, each with its time and age.
A bound session texts you build is green with messaging_send; a session without an out binding is refused.
how_to: Open settings, notifications, messaging and press add provider. Enter the bridge address, its token (or an op:// reference) and your phone number or email; allow a private address and plain http only for a bridge on your own network. Save: Carnivore checks the bridge first.
On the provider, press add conversation and add the conversation with you; only conversations the bridge lists as routable can be added.
Ask an agent with the messaging tools to bind the session to the conversation (it names a direction: in and out, in only or out only); you approve the bind when it asks.
Text the conversation from your phone. Start with @name to reach one session when several are bound, or reply to a session's own text.
Watch the log on the settings screen for held and failed messages; retry a failed one there.
A text you sent whose outcome is unknown (the bridge restarted mid-send) shows in the log as unconfirmed, in its own color, with no retry: check your phone before sending it again.
On the provider card, the duplicate-send protection line says whether a retried send was ever answered with the original result (proven, with when) or never seen yet.

catalog.description: Below 769px a strip of keys sits under the terminal: slash commands, esc, tab, the four arrows, the terminal tools menu and Enter. Drag the strip up and it snaps open to twice its height in 250 ms to show a second row: the agent key (shift tab, cycles permission mode), undo (control shift minus), search, sleep, session theme, session notes, keep awake, session files and session plugins. Each of those runs the same action the desktop toolbar and header run. Drag down to snap back to one row. A plain tap on a key never counts as a drag. Open or closed is remembered on this device, and the terminal refits once after the animation ends.
examples: Answer a prompt with Enter without opening the phone keyboard.
Put the session to sleep from the phone without opening the menu.
how_to: Drag the strip up (or flick it) to show the second row.
Drag it down to go back to one row.
Tap Enter in the first row to send a return to the terminal.
In the second row, tap undo to send control shift minus, stash to stash the current prompt (control s), or sleep, theme, notes, keep awake, files or search for the same actions as on desktop.
