catalog.description: Twelve kinds of destination, many instances of each: slack, discord, microsoft teams (workflows webhook), telegram, ntfy, pushover, a generic signed webhook, email (smtp), sms through aws sns, sms through twilio, pagerduty, and every web push device. Every secret, recipient and number lives in the Keychain and is write-only. One matrix lists 29 notification types in families (needs you, sessions, accounts, health, app, in-app only) against a screen column plus one column per destination. Every cell can be unticked, needs-you included; needs-you starts ticked. Hiding a card hides the pop-up only: the bell, the history, the status light and the tray keep everything. Each destination can add away mode, quiet hours, a reminder and a project filter, and can opt in to details (tool and target, or the question snippet; scrubbed, capped at 200 characters, never on sms). The message carries a link back, tried in order: the mobile sync public address, then the local name, then the network address, then no link. A pause switch holds all outside delivery on one computer. Settings and secrets sync to paired computers over the paired link, secrets landing in each computer's Keychain; any tick or destination can be pinned to one computer. An agent can send you a notification with the notify tool. The old Slack, ntfy and Pushover secrets move into the Keychain.
examples: You walk away from your desk: the permission and question notifications go to your phone through ntfy or Pushover, and a quiet-hours window keeps the finished-turn pings off at night while a permission request still gets through.
A shared channel gets a Slack message when a session dies, but with details off, so no command or file name leaves the computer.
Your laptop and your desktop are paired: add a destination once and it appears on both, with its secret stored in each computer's Keychain.
A destination fails five times in a row with a permanent error: it is switched off and a notifications health alert tells you, without that alert being sent outside.

Home Assistant at http://homeassistant.local:8123 receives your session notifications through a webhook, with plain http turned on for this computer only; the same destination synced to your laptop sits quietly there with a note that plain http is off on that computer, and is never switched off for it.
how_to: Open settings, notifications, destinations, press add a destination, pick a kind from the grouped list (each service has its logo; click the field or use the arrow keys, type to filter), fill in its fields and press add. Secrets are write-only: once saved they show as set, and a blank field keeps the stored one. A webhook generates a signing secret for you and shows it once.
Press test on a destination to send one fixed test message; one test every 10 seconds.

Open settings, notifications, routing. Tick a notification under a destination to send it there. The screen column decides which cards pop up; needs-you rows start ticked and can be unticked like any other. A tick on the new destination column sets what a new destination starts with.
Turn on this computer only, then change a tick: it is pinned here with a local badge and does not sync. Press reset to global on a pinned cell to go back to the synced value.

On a destination, set away mode (hold a notification while you are active at this computer, and send it once you are away), quiet hours (needs-you notifications still go through), a reminder (minutes, or off) and a project filter (empty means all projects). Turn on details to add the tool and target or the question snippet; sms never gets details.

Under routing, read the link line: it says which link outside messages carry (mobile sync address, local name, network address or none) and why. Use the pause switch to hold all outside delivery on this computer.
With a paired computer, settings and secrets sync over the paired link, and each computer keeps secrets in its own Keychain. Pin an item to keep this computer's value.

An agent in a session can call the notify tool to send you one notification of type agent.message, routed by the matrix. The switch is mcp.agent_notify (PUT /api/v1/mcp-admin/agent-notify); off hides the tool.
Existing Slack, ntfy and Pushover settings move into Keychain-backed destinations on their own and the plaintext is removed from config.json and its backup.

A self-hosted webhook or ntfy server that only speaks http (n8n, Home Assistant) on your own network: on its form turn on allow private addresses, then allow plain http on this network, and use an http:// address. Both switches are for this computer only and never sync. While plain http is on, the message and any auth header cross your network unencrypted; only private addresses are allowed, and a public address stays refused.

catalog.description: The nudge is part of the Task Manager plugin again (it was its own plugin from 2026-10-12 to 2026-10-16). It ships off: its own switch, 'send nudges to idle agents', is in the Task Manager's settings, and with it off no nudge is sent and nothing runs; turn it on and it starts without a restart. It also stops whenever the Task Manager plugin is off. Its timers (minutes of silence, nudges before an item is flagged, items named per nudge) and the three nudge texts are settings in the Task Manager's side pane, under the same names as before. What you saved under the old nudge plugin carries over once, when the app first starts after the change.
examples: You turn the nudge on, switch it on for a project, and an item that sat open for an hour gets its idle agent woken with your own wording.
You lower the tries to two so a stuck item asks you to unstick it sooner.
You turn the nudge switch off while you are away from the desk; no agent is woken and no nudge line is posted until you turn it on again.
how_to: Open the plugins page from the menu tab, open the Task Manager's settings and turn on 'send nudges to idle agents'.
Set the minutes of silence before a nudge, how many nudges an item gets before it asks you to unstick it, and how many items one nudge names.
Edit the three nudge texts to change what the agent is told; the slots {minutes}, {item}, {items}, {is} and {it} are filled in, and an empty text brings back the standard words.

catalog.description: A file opened from the files widget is a row of the left sidebar's own files list, right under the browsers, and shows full size in the main section where a browser page shows. One row per file per session, the path on the file mark's tooltip and a dot while it has unsaved edits. The row behaves like every other opened item: click shows it, the kebab closes it, and holding Shift turns the kebab into a red x. Closing a file with unsaved edits asks first. A save is refused when the file changed on disk after it was opened (an agent wrote it), with keep editing, reload from disk and overwrite. A binary, a file over 2 MB or a file that is gone shows a plain can't show line, and a changed file's diff shows read only. The files widget also accepts a pasted absolute or ~/ file path, including outside the selected project and without a session. Markdown opens in rendered preview with an edit toggle.
examples: Open main.py from the files widget: a files row appears under the browsers and the file fills the main section, with the session's rails still around it.
An agent edits the file while you have it open: your save is refused, and you pick reload from disk or overwrite.
Close a file with unsaved edits by holding Shift and clicking the red x: it asks before throwing the edits away.
Click a changed file in the files widget's changed files tab: its diff opens read only in the main section.
An agent opens plan.md with color cyan and icon docs: the row in the files list wears a cyan docs icon and name.
Paste a path to /Users/you/notes.plan.markdown while no session is selected: its file row opens in rendered preview, then edit and save through the usual stale-save guard.
how_to: Open the files widget (the files key on the right widget bar, or a files component), then click a file, a changed file's open, or a changed file itself for its diff.
Press open path in the files widget, paste an absolute or ~/ path on this computer, then open file. Markdown starts in preview; choose edit to change it.
Edit and press save, or Cmd or Ctrl+S; a markdown file has a preview toggle.
Switch between open files from the files list in the left sidebar; unsaved edits stay with each row until you save or close it.
GET /api/v1/files/open lists the rows; POST opens one; DELETE /api/v1/files/open/{id} closes one; GET and PUT /api/v1/files/open/{id}/content read and save with the sha256 revision check.

An agent opens a file for you with the MCP tool files_open (target, path, root, kind, and optional color and icon); it adds or reuses the row and does not switch your screen unless it also sets front true.
To make a row easier to spot, an agent can give it a theme color and an icon when it opens it, or later with sidebar_row_look_set (row, color, icon); a row with neither looks as before.

catalog.description: Code reaches another paired computer by the ladder: git remote clone, then incremental git bundles carried over the Pack link into refs/carnivore/<install>/..., then a one-way tar.zst that includes uncommitted work. An air-gapped project never contacts GitHub. Each project resolves which GitHub account to use, and every gh or git call names it. A private repo can be published on the owner's click. A gh login can be carried to a paired computer whose owner allowed it.
examples: Send a commit to another computer with no remote at all.
Carry the example-owner gh login to studio so it can pull private repos.
how_to: POST /api/v1/projects/{name}/sync with a paired computer to carry the project's code.
POST /api/v1/projects/{name}/publish-repo to create a private repo.

how_to: On by default for every account: an account the owner has not switched off is sent to every paired computer whose own owner allows receiving credentials. The owner can switch an account off in the app (pack, logins tab, credential relay).
Only the computer that owns the login ever refreshes it; the other computers receive a fresh access token and its expiry, never the refresh token.

A receiving computer keeps the copy in its own relay profile, never in a login someone made there, and receives it only after its own owner turns on may receive credentials (off by default; this did not change).

The receiving computer's owner accepts logins per account: all of them, only a named list, or none. Until it answers, nothing is written there; an account offered later under a named list waits as pending. Owner only, no mcp tool.

A popup in the middle of the screen asks for that answer the first time a paired computer offers a login: yes or no, with no way to dismiss it, and a checklist of the offered accounts (all ticked) plus an all accounts box that also covers accounts added later. Change it any time under pack, logins, this computer receives.

how_to: Open the pack row in the menu (press h with the menu focused). The computers tab lists every computer once, this computer first: its name, the alpha badge, a green computer icon for this computer, a two-computers icon for the link (green while the computer answers, grey within about half a minute of it going quiet), model and cores, cpu, memory and disk as segmented meters, and the installed tools row.

A meter is 20 cells outlined in a hairline: green under 75 percent, amber from 75, coral from 90. The compute reserve shows as a hatched zone at the top end of the bar. cpu is the 1 minute load average over the cores, so 5/10 is load 5 on 10 cores.

Press make alpha next to a computer's name, on the computer that is alpha now, to hand alpha to another computer; every paired computer follows within seconds, because each one accepts only a change signed by the alpha it follows. Pressed on any other computer it changes only that computer, and the others raise a refused pack change alert offering to follow it there.

On the work tab: a status strip (the alpha, computers online, whether this computer follows it) and the follow the alpha switch with a more disclosure; placement with spread work across the pack and enhanced placement (changed on alpha; elsewhere the change is refused as not alpha), whose connection and model pickers appear inline while it is on and state the default in the field; per computer, its real compute reserve and restrictions as chips with edit opening the editor in place; and move a project or company, which needs both the project and the target computer before the move button enables.
Restrictions on another computer can only be tightened from here; that computer's own owner loosens them.
On the logins tab: switch the credential relay on per Claude account, and this computer's own may receive credentials switch.

catalog.description: A migrate plans first (the code rung, what is blocking, what moves), then copies the code, Swarm agents with their memory, task manager threads and cards, and the conversation files to the other computer, which checks everything before it becomes the project's home. The old copy stays here, inactive and marked moved away, and one call brings the project back. Nothing runs while a session or agent is live under the project, and the other computer's own restrictions decide whether it accepts.

catalog.description: The Swarm page opens from the swarm page link on the drawer's task manager panel (or the #swarm link) and leaves the drawer on its tab. Its ledger lists SysOp, companies, projects, agents and your ordinary sessions as collapsible rows; the org chart draws the same tree top-down with zoom and pan, stacking each parent's leaf agents in a column (two or three when long) so it grows down instead of sideways and never shrinks to fit; nodes is the drawer panel at full width. All three show the same active floor, with one quiet link to show the inactive ones, and all three follow the node filter, which shows one node's lineage: the node, its parents up to SysOp and everything under it. An agent's chat groups its messages in bursts: one header per run from the same sender (an arrow in for what the agent received, out for what it sent, the sender's square, its name and the time since), follow-ups tucked under it with only a dim time, two or more quiet events in a row folded into one "N events" line that opens in place, and a question or review card always under its own header with a yellow edge; an outgoing crosstalk message is headed by the agent it went to. A click on an agent anywhere (a ledger row, a node, a square, a name in a chat message, an agent row in the task manager) slides its chat out and leaves whatever you were looking at on screen (a terminal, a page, the swarm page itself): at 1024 px and wider the chat docks and that view gets narrower to fit beside it, and closing the chat gives the width back; narrower windows show the chat over it. The agent's terminal opens only from the chat's own agent terminal control, and a click never wakes an agent. On the nodes and org chart tabs a shift+click filters to that node's lineage (shift+click it again to clear); the filtered node keeps an outline. A company or project with no agent is a vacant seat that asks before turning one on. The settings tab picks the default view, the default density and the character set. Project, company and SysOp nodes wear the same rolled-up status the Agents tab heading shows, and a vacant seat takes that status's hue on its dashed outline. Every project, company and SysOp wears its own bright color, as unlike the others as the screen allows on the theme you are using (each new one picked as the color farthest from every one before it, so adding one never moves the rest; dark and light themes get their own sets, neons and near-whites included), and only a project's agents and sessions share its tone, each a distinct bright shade, never a muddy one; a color you set by hand on an agent still wins. Its settings tab also sets the Swarm look for every device: agent colors by project or random, a body shape per agent type and an animation per status.
examples: see every active agent and who it reports to at a glance
turn on an agent for a project that has none by clicking its vacant seat
tell at a glance which project an agent belongs to by its color tone
make companies hexagons and sysop a cloud, or let every agent wear its own random color

scroll the wheel or press plus and minus on the org chart to zoom, drag to pan

open an agent's chat, then use its menu (the kebab, a right click on its title strip, or Shift+F10) to pop it out into its own window or make it a widget, or drag its title row onto the layout to drop it as a widget

a swarm agent in a folder carnivore made (alpha, a company hq, a project you approved) is trusted for you on every account; a folder of your own still shows one trust card per start, and clicking it answers claude code's question

in an agent's chat, every message starts with the name of who posted it (or you) and how long ago; rest the pointer on the name or on an agent's square (the big one beside a message or the tiny one inside a sent message) to see its company / project / name, and click it to open that agent's terminal in the middle of the page, as the war room does

catalog.description: Each project and company gets a uid that never changes and is the same on every computer holding it. A project has a home (the computer holding the project of record), may have active replicas on paired computers (same uid, nothing locked, both run at once), and may be moved away, the source of a one-way migrate. A moved-away project is the only locked state: every session create and every wake inside its folder is refused with 409 project_moved_away, and the drawer heading and the Projects page say moved to the computer's name. Replicas are made from the project's own routes and registered on the other computer through a peer-only route that needs the replica scope. A project can be marked air-gapped so Carnivore never contacts GitHub for it.

catalog.description: Move waits for the session's current turn to end, never interrupting it, then sleeps the session, carries its conversation to the other computer and wakes it there resumed in the same conversation. The other computer checks first, before anything moves, that it allows the session's project and has a login that can run the session's account, and refuses with the reason named. The old row is archived once the new one is awake and a forward record names the new computer; the moved session appears through the paired computer's listing.
examples: Move the build session to studio while it finishes its current turn.
how_to: Open a session row menu, choose move to another computer, pick the paired computer and confirm; the move starts when the turn ends.

catalog.description: A send does one of three things on a paired computer. Move is the session move: the agent stops here and continues there with its conversation. Copy waits for the current turn to end, carries a whole-lines snapshot of the conversation and starts a new session there that resumes it as a fork with its own conversation id, while the original keeps running untouched; the code keeps syncing both ways: when either agent finishes a turn its new commits go to the other computer, which fast-forwards its checked-out branch only when its agent is idle, its tree is clean and the move is a pure fast-forward. Fresh starts a new agent in the same project on that computer with no conversation. When the other computer does not hold the project yet, with_project adds it as a replica and syncs it first; without that the refusal stays project_not_on_target. The other computer decides every refusal by its own restrictions. A check route reports per mode what would work, with no side effects, and progress is a pack op. Before you confirm, the send dialog shows a plain checklist: what comes along, what stays behind and why (uncommitted work, ignored folders with their size, another project's folders), tools the conversation ran that the other computer lacks, and servers that will stop. Folders outside the project that the agent used are read from the conversation since its last compaction; a computer that cannot take them yet says to update it.
examples: Copy the build agent to studio: row menu, send to, studio, copy it, send. The original keeps running here.
An agent ran python3 -m http.server 5041 and used a scratch folder: the dialog lists the folder (ticked when under 500 mb and the computer can take it) and says the server on port 5041 will stop.
how_to: Open an agent's row menu, choose send to, then a computer. Pick move it, copy it, start a new agent there, or move the whole project; tick "copy the project to <computer> first" when the project is not there yet; press send.
Read the checklist under the options before pressing send: it lists what comes along, what stays behind, missing tools (a warning, never a refusal) and servers that will stop.

catalog.description: The pipeline widget came back 2026-10-12 on the owner's request ("yes bring them back", #1689) after the other operator's #1682 U1 removed the old job version. It is global only, off the surface until you place it, and it draws the new engine. On top is a row of status squares (item 519), one per plugin the engine runs (stats, deep search, and any later one), each showing its state by shape as well as color the way the old job widget did: a filled green circle caught up, a yellow ring behind, a coral diamond failing, a gray dash when the engine is off; a rebuild shows as behind and says rebuilding. Hovering a square, focusing it with the keyboard or tapping it opens its detail: how many files wait and how old the oldest is, when it last delivered, its last error and how many are failing, and how many runs since the server started. The squares carry no rebuild button (2026-10-12): a rebuild is done from Settings, pipeline. The overall status line (caught up, behind, stalled, rebuilding or off) sits small beside the row. Under it are two short sections (2026-10-12): running lists each plugin on the transcript being delivered right now (and any rebuild in progress) with its area and how long it has run, ticking in the browser; queue lists the next transcripts waiting in the order the engine takes them, at most eight and then "+N more", each for all plugins or the one plugin whose retry holds it, with its area (a live transcript whose session name is not known yet shows its short id) and how long it has waited, or when its retry is due. The engine announces a delivery when it starts as well as when the batch ends, so running shows without polling. Under those is the pipeline chart (item 542, #1701): one row per area and plugin, updated in place rather than a row per run, with the plugin's friendly name, its area (the session's name, else the project's, else machine for work with no session such as a catch-up scan of an old conversation or a rebuild), how long the last run took, how long ago that was (ticking in the browser with no request) and how many runs since the server started. A failed run wears a diamond mark, a parked one a dash. Every figure column keeps the room its widest value needs, so the run time is never cut off; the name and area give way first, and a very narrow widget drops the runs and then the area before any figure. The server keeps these rows in memory only (about 100, empty after a restart); it records and logs, it never alerts. Every view shares one read of GET /api/v1/pipeline/status, pushed on the pipeline topic after every batch, park, scan pass and rebuild, so nothing polls while the live connection is up (a 10 second poll runs only while it is down). The developer widget carries it as its pipeline tab. While the conversation backups plugin is on, the chart also shows a backups row (area conversations, #1807): its 30 minute passes plus the captures on close, sleep, restart, clear and fork as runs, the last run's time and duration, and a failed mark when the latest pass or capture failed; with the plugin off the row is not there. It comes through a plugin seam (src/cplugs/sdk/pipeline_rows.py), so the plugin stays self contained.
examples: See at a glance which plugin is behind or failing by the shape of its square.
See at once whether deep search is behind and by how many files.

catalog.description: Every plugin built into this app, on the shared manager frame, one kind of row with one switch each. A plugin that is switched off stops contributing to every surface it adds to (the session row menu, a tab, a menu link). Mark unread and share read only are plugins that ship on; task manager ships on for a clean install and keeps an existing install's choice. The choice is stored on the server, so every device agrees. Built-in plugins are part of the app, so none of those can be installed or removed here. Store plugins from the catalog sit on the same page as the same card warez draws (hero image on top, same order as warez): a plugin that is not installed shows the same add control as warez (add, with its caret to pick global or a project), a plugin with an update due shows update, and only an installed plugin shows its switch, which turns it off for the picked project. A plugin that runs a program (an MCP server) prints the full command on its card; add goes through warez's one-click route and opens the install sheet when the server asks for consent. Turning one on grants what it asks, listed in its details. The details are tabbed: overview, settings, permissions and data, with the state and switch always at the top and a plain reason when a plugin is held or waiting for a grant. Each permission is shown by risk tier, a plugin that asks for something dangerous in combination carries a warning, and a plugin's recent permission use is listed in its details. An agent can turn a plugin off or revoke grants over MCP, never turn one on or add a grant.
examples: Turn off share read only on a computer where nobody should hand out spectator links.
Turn off mark unread if you never use it and want a shorter session menu.
Turn on task manager to get the shared list between you and claude.
Search 'joe' to find the plugins Joe wrote, or 'tab' to find the plugins that add a tab.
On a phone the page is one bar: the back arrow at the left, the title over the search in one frame, the filters that fit and one grid/list flip at the right.
Turn on flow chart while the swarm plugin is off and see it wait for it: turn the swarm plugin on and it starts.
Open mcp health, press the data tab and purge it while it is off: its folder, settings, grants and stored secrets go, and a plugin that ships on comes back on.
Press add on the rea card, or its caret to pick a project: the same control warez draws. Once installed it shows its switch; switch it off and it is gone from the picked project.
how_to: Open the menu tab of the agents drawer and choose plugins, or press view all on the plugins card.
Search, pick a state (all, on, off) from the state facet, or sort by name or on first in the toolbar; press its name for its details.
Press its switch to turn it on or off; turning one on grants what its details say it asks.
Each plugin is one 28px row with its switch first and no repeated kind mark; press the name or the row to open its details. What this page cannot do is in the (i) beside the count.
Use the grid and list buttons at the right of the search bar to switch views; the choice is remembered on this device. Grid is the default.
On a phone, the back arrow at the top left leaves the page; the search sits beside the title and the filters and grid/list toggle share the one row below.

A plugin's details are four tabs under a strip with its name, state and switch: overview, settings, permissions and data. Arrow keys move between the tabs, and the tab you pick stays picked as you open other plugins, remembered on this device.

A plugin that has settings shows a gear on its card: press it to open the plugin's details on the settings tab. The same pane opens from #plugins/<plugin id>/settings. Plugin settings are not in the app Settings: restore points (save), the conversation index and usage stats keep their panels in their own details too.

A plugin waiting on a grant, or held because it could not start, shows a yellow strip under its name saying why. Press review to open its permissions tab: each permission is listed by risk with granted or not granted; tick each medium and high one yourself, there is no tick-all, then press grant. The tab also lists what the plugin used lately.

A plugin that is on but needs another plugin that is off reads on, but doing nothing until a plugin it needs is on, and its details list what it is waiting for (the swarm plugin, for flow chart and nudge).

A plugin's details list its dependencies: what it needs (other plugins, app features such as crosstalk or the save pipeline, the minimum app version), each marked ok, off or missing, and which plugins need it. A missing app feature or too old an app refuses turning it on and says why. Turning off a plugin that other plugins need asks first and names them.

The data tab shows how much the plugin stores and its folder. Purge data asks first with the number of files and the size, and only deletes when you confirm; it is off while the plugin is on, so turn it off first.
Store plugins: press add on a card (the caret picks global or a project), or update when one is due. An installed plugin shows its switch; switching off removes it from the picked project only.

catalog.description: Public review links is a plugin, off by default, that will let people outside your network open one review board through your own reverse proxy, look at it, and leave answers and comments, and nothing else. This first version only builds the guarded door. When you turn it on and fill in a port, a bind address, your public host name and your proxy's address, it opens a second small listener that answers not found to every request, because no links exist yet. Before a request is looked at, the door checks that it comes from your proxy, names your host, has a plain path with no encodings, dot segments or query, and matches an exact route; websockets and protocol upgrades are never accepted, bodies and headers are capped, and every answer carries the strict security headers. Turning the plugin off closes the socket.
examples: With the plugin on and a proxy address set, any request from another computer gets a 403 and a request with the wrong host name gets a 421.
A request for any path, even a valid-looking one, gets the same empty 404 until links ship in a later version.
how_to: Turn on the review board plugin, then public review links, on the plugins page.
Set the port, the one address to listen on, your public host name and your reverse proxy's exact address in the plugin's settings.
Point your proxy at that address and port. Turning the plugin off closes the port.

A click on an approval opens the approval inbox on that session; a click on a task manager item shows it in the task manager through the documented focus route; a click on an alert opens the bell's panel. In the drawer widget area and the session rails the widget can be placed more than once, and each copy has a checkmark for every type (approvals, task manager questions and each sender the alert center knows), all on until you switch one off; a copy that lists exactly one type wears that type's icon and name, and a copy that lists several wears an inbox-tray icon. A counts switch in the same options panel (on by default) shows or hides that copy's number on its sidebar icon and the count at the top of the widget. A quiet day reads nothing waiting on you. It fits the home grid, the terminal page and the drawer widget area from 220px wide.

catalog.description: Stage one of driving sessions on another machine you can ssh into, with nothing installed there. This first slice lands the host dimension: a `hosts` table (schema v40) with this machine as `local`, a host on every session and project (all `local` until the remote backend lands), and the routes to add, list, edit and remove a machine by its ssh target. The second slice adds the ssh transport and a probe that checks a host over ssh (tmux and its version, the login shell, the agents, whether the far box runs its own Carnivore) and stores what it found. Alex's rulings D1 to D5 and the slices: `docs/remote-hosts.md`. The third step runs sessions there: `POST /sessions` with a `host_key` creates a session in a folder on that machine (connecting it on first use), its output streams back while you watch, and closing it kills it on that machine only; a session on this machine with the same name is never touched.
examples: Add the studio computer from the hosts page, probe it to check ssh, tmux and the agents it has, then pick it in the new-session dialog to launch a claude session there.
Script your machines through the API instead of the page: one POST per box; the hosts page reads and writes the same routes.
Pair the studio computer from the discovered list with one click, then revoke the grant you gave it when it is sold, or unpair to end both sides at once.
how_to: Open Pack (press h with the drawer menu focused, or go to /#hosts), open the computers tab, and press "add a computer" for a label and an ssh target (an alias from your ~/.ssh/config, or user@host); the port and tmux socket are optional. The server generates the host's key; it shows up in the detail pane once the host is added.

Open the new row and press "probe" to check it over ssh: tmux and its version, the login shell, the agents it has, and whether it runs its own Carnivore. A failed probe names why (unreachable, ssh authentication failed, host key not verified, tmux too old); fix it and probe again.
Turn a host off with its switch (never on this machine), or remove it once no session names it (never this machine either).
Pick the host when you start a new session: the picker is skipped straight to this machine while no other host is configured, and only asks once you have added one.

A remote session's row carries its host's label beside its status light in the drawer, dimmed when the host is degraded or offline; this machine's own rows show no host label at all. Its status is read off its own pane (a permission dialog there reads question), with host_state down and status unknown while its host is unreachable; after a restart it comes back on its row and id.

Rename a remote session, pin it a theme or give it its own terminal background from its row menu and header exactly as a local one; each is kept for that host's session alone, never for a same-named session on this machine. Restart it from its row menu (the picker previews its far pane), or restart a stopped one from the launchpad: it comes back on its host, on the same row, resuming its conversation, but only once the host is reachable and confirms the old session is gone. Fork and sleep act on this machine and are not offered on a remote row.

Or drive it through the API directly: POST /api/v1/hosts to add, GET to list, PATCH to edit, DELETE to remove, POST /api/v1/hosts/{key}/probe to check it, and POST /sessions with host_key set to a probed host to launch there.

Pair with another computer running Carnivore: it appears under "found on this network" on the hosts page (Bonjour); open it and press "pair". If its ssh host key is already trusted here nothing is typed and the pairing finishes; on first contact the dialog asks for a code, which you get by pressing "show a code" on the other computer's own hosts page and typing its pairing id and code here. A computer Bonjour cannot see (a tailnet, another network) is added with "pair a computer": its name or ssh target.

A paired computer shows one of: connected, connecting, disconnected (the link is down and retrying), incompatible (its carnivore speaks another protocol), unpaired (it dropped its grant) or identity changed (its key is not the pinned one: unpair and pair again). A computer that is both an ssh host and a paired computer sits under one heading. Its detail pane lists the grants this computer issued to it with revoke on each (that computer still sees this one until it revokes its own), and unpair, which ends both sides.

The toolbar holds the advertise switch (on by default; off stops this computer announcing itself, browsing stays), a rescan, and "rotate key", which asks first and tells every connected computer; a computer that was offline must pair again.

catalog.description: The review board is a plugin (off by default, needs the task manager) for mockups that go through rounds of review. A board is one folder in a git checkout: a sidecar file and one immutable page per revision, so the folder alone rebuilds the board. The read side is: the boards folder setting (it must be a real folder holding a .boards-root file, inside a git checkout, and never the app copy, an app bundle or the app state folder), the list of boards with whose turn each is in (your turn, with claude, undelivered), one board in full with the rounds you sent word for word, a rescan after a hand edit or a git pull, and two agent tools to read them. The board page shows a board read only: a title strip with whose turn it is, a history bar of revisions with the rounds you sent as diamonds between them, and the mockup itself in a locked-down frame (scripts run, but it has no network, storage or login, and it can only point at tagged parts of the page). You can step through revisions, switch between the real width and a fit-to-width view, and pop the page out into a tab of its own. Claude opens a board on your screen with task_manager_board_focus. Claude publishes boards and revisions: task_manager_board_create starts a board for a task and task_manager_board_revision_add adds each next revision (a page, a summary and the prompts to answer); every revision posts a card on the task and by default puts the task in review. A revision's files are never changed once written, and a failed write leaves the board as it was. Slice 5 adds Joe's review loop: a prompt fold-down under the board header where he ticks, checks and writes notes, drafts kept on the server, a send that lands on the task as his reply once even if sent twice, a round card on the task, diamonds on the history bar, resend and relink for a round that did not get through, ghost lines for a question asked again, and flip. A revision may instead own its controls (payload_mode): the page posts its state, the board header has a draft light, a save stepper, a note for the agent and send, there is no sidebar, the page's state autosaves as one overwriting draft, every send makes a numbered save and only nudges the session to review the payload, and a theme picker repaints just the page in another Carnivore theme. Closed reviews: a board whose task is done is closed (derived on read, never stored, so reopening the task reopens it), and each project's page on the projects page has a closed reviews group listing them, newest closed first, while the plugin is on. A revision may also name a questions layer (task_manager_board_create and task_manager_board_revision_add take layer): claude sends a list of questions instead of writing the controls, and the board draws them inside the frame, with no page needed. The fields are yes or no, pick one, pick several, on or off, a short text and a long text, and each question has a small note key. Questions sit right under the part of the page they ask about, the rest in one section at the end, or all in one panel at the edge of the frame (a bottom sheet on a phone). Your answers autosave, step through saves and send exactly like a payload page, and arrive as values and notes keyed by the question ids.

Pick another theme in the header and only the page repaints.

Claude asks 'keep the rail?' (yes or no), 'density' (pick one) and 'why' (long text) in a layer with no page; you answer, add a note on the first, and Send; Claude reads {values: {...}, notes: {...}} on the round.

Claude posts 40 findings as a rows layer; each row shows what you had, what it is now and Claude's take (marked, not picked), you pick fine, push back or decide later on each, add a note on two, and Send; Claude reads values and notes keyed by row id.

Claude demos a layout live: you watch the page change on each call, say 'bookmark that' when you like one, and the draft is kept as a named revision that asks for your review; with inline_picks on, the prompts sit right under their rows on the page.
how_to: Turn the review board on from the plugins page (it needs the task manager) and set the task manager folder (the boardsRoot setting) to an absolute path. New boards, and the pastes and artifacts of every task, are saved under it in a folder per project, then per task.
Call task_manager_boards_list, optionally with task set to a task manager item id, then task_manager_board_get with the slug.
After a hand edit or a git pull, POST /api/v1/cplugs/reviewboard/rescan reads the folder again.

Claude starts a board with task_manager_board_create (name, title, task, summary, html or file_path, viewport, prompts) and adds revisions with task_manager_board_revision_add; set request_review to false to post the card without putting the task in review.

Claude opens a board on your screen with task_manager_board_focus (board, optional revision); or open the review tab from the open menu and pick a board. Use the arrows or the history bar to move between revisions, the fit icon to switch between real width and fit, and the pop-out icon for a tab of its own.

On a board that asks prompts, press the prompts key in the header (it shows how many are unanswered): a panel folds down under the header. Tap an option, tick a check, write a note or pin one to a part of the mockup, then press the send icon. The line under it names the task it went to. A diamond on the history bar opens the round as you sent it; if it says not delivered, press resend or link the board to another task with the link icon. The flip icon swaps the mockup between this revision and the one before.

A scratch board takes a page plus its files in one call, with no approval, even from an owner-minted token (your phone): task_manager_scratch_post (name, html or file_path, files as [{name, content_base64}], or file_paths for a session on this computer). The page shows a file by naming it files/<name>. The first post with a name files a Scratch task and makes the board; later posts add revisions. A script can POST the same as multipart to /api/v1/cplugs/reviewboard/scratch. Clear it for good with the trash key on the board's title strip.

A payload board: Claude publishes a revision with payload_mode true, a page with its own controls (a list with checkboxes, say) that posts its state to the board. There is no sidebar: the page has the full width and the header carries a light that says saved, saving or not saved with the reason, arrows that step through every numbered save and back to the draft, a note key for the agent ('look at my changes and direct me') and send. The page's state is saved automatically as one draft that is overwritten in place (kept in the sidecar, written a moment after you stop and when you leave), and reopening the board loads it back. Send is your press only: it makes the next numbered save, records a round with the state, your note and what changed since your last send, and nudges the session to review the payload; it does not paste the payload.

The theme picker in the header lists the Carnivore themes; the first entry follows the app's theme. Choosing one repaints only the page frame (the app around it does not change) and is remembered on this device.

Claude attaches files to a board with task_manager_board_attachment_add (board, files as [{name, content_base64}] or file_paths for a session on this computer, an optional note, request_review default true). The files are saved on the board's task with one info naming them, and the task goes to review. A script can POST the same JSON to /api/v1/cplugs/reviewboard/boards/{slug}/attachments. A scratch board takes no attachments.

On the board page, the paperclip key in the header shows how many files are attached; press it for the list, newest first, with each file's size, date and revision, and keys to open it in a new tab or download it.

Press the note key in the board header to open the notes panel in the top right corner. Write markdown, switch to preview, and press ? for the list of what the preview understands. Drag the bottom left corner to resize it; the size is kept on this device. The words survive a reload: a prompt board keeps them in its draft, a payload board in this browser, until a send goes through. On a phone it opens as a sheet from the bottom.

With the review board on, open a project on the projects page: under its session groups a closed reviews group lists that project's boards whose task is done (ticked), newest closed first, each with its task, revision count and how long ago it closed. Unfold it, press show all for the rest, and tap a row or open to bring the board back up as a page row. Reopen the task and the board leaves the group. Agents ask task_manager_boards_list with state closed and project set to the project's id.

Claude calls task_manager_board_create or task_manager_board_revision_add with layer {kind: questions, v: 1, title, items: [...]} and no html. Answer in the frame; each question has a note key. Your answers autosave as the draft and Send hands them back to Claude as values and notes.

Claude runs a board live with task_manager_board_live_set (each call overwrites one working draft: no new revision, no card, the task stays where it is); say 'bookmark that' (task_manager_board_milestone_add) to freeze the draft as a named revision, and task_manager_board_live_stop ends the session. The board header shows a live mark, a bookmark key and an end key.

catalog.description: The file browser has two tabs. 'files' is the tree, where every changed entry has its name tinted by status and one letter at the right edge (U untracked, M modified, A added, D deleted, R renamed, ! conflict), and a folder holding changes takes its strongest child's tint and a dot. 'changed files' lists every changed path with its letter, in git's order, with '+N more' past the cap. A status line pinned to the bottom of the browser shows the repository, branch, a dirty dot, ahead and behind, the staged, modified and untracked counts and the last commit's short sha. The repository is read only while the browser is open and stays live as the files change. catalog.description: A widget for any widget bar. It follows the session the bar is showing and reads its files once when you switch session, and again when you press refresh; it never polls. For a Claude session it lists the CLAUDE.md chain (the account's own, each folder from the working directory up, CLAUDE.local.md, rules and what they import), skills, agents, commands, hooks, output styles, settings layers (global, project, project local, managed), MCP servers (user, local, project .mcp.json, plugin) and installed plugins. For a Codex session it lists the AGENTS.md chain, skills, prompts, config.toml settings, profiles and MCP servers. Each row shows the name, its line count and G (global), P (project) or PL (plugin); press a row to select it and open its file in the Files tab, and see its full path, kind, line count and load status (loaded, available to load or disabled) in the details footer. An item with no file of its own, such as an MCP server or a settings key, only selects. A filter box narrows the open sections, and a show path key swaps each name for its path. The title row has a scope toggle that cycles local (this project), global (the account) and all, and the icon menu and right-click menu carry the same choices plus refresh; each copy keeps its own scope. Each section folds from its header and shows its count. Line counts are not context tokens. The files are read from the session's own account config folder, so a session on a second account shows that account's skills. It shows names, paths and descriptions only: never an env value, token, header or URL, and Codex's auth file is never opened. A session on a paired computer says to open its contents there.

catalog.description: The attention watcher reads the session's own transcript once per cycle, a bounded amount at a time, and counts skill use: a Skill tool call, a skill run as a slash command, or, for Codex, a read of a SKILL.md, which is only inferred and is labelled that way. Only the skill name, the time and how it was seen are kept, in a small local file that can be deleted and rebuilt at any time; no message text is stored and nothing leaves the machine. The session listing carries the count and the newest skill; a session whose transcript cannot be read has no count, never zero. Claude Code's own commands such as clear and model are not counted. Nothing here feeds the light's colour or the auto-sleep idle clock.

how_to: Open the session's menu (three dots on its drawer row) and choose sleep agent.
The agent stops and its terminal closes; the row stays where it was, showing a moon.
To bring it back, open the same menu and choose wake agent. It resumes the same conversation.
A session whose agent exited on its own (/exit, Ctrl-C or a crash) also shows a moon. Wake brings it back in its own terminal, resuming the same conversation; nothing running is stopped.

catalog.description: Claude Code records the scheduling a session does for itself as tool calls in its own transcript: a self wakeup (the /loop mechanism) and session-only cron jobs, which a later call can cancel. The attention watcher reads them from the session's current conversation once per cycle and counts a timer as live only while the claude process that set it is alive and started before it, because these timers live inside that process and die with it. The session listing carries the live count and the soonest fire time; a codex or shell session is not applicable, never zero. A clock chip beside the subagent chip shows the time to the next fire (18m, 3h, due) or the live count, in the agents drawer (cozy and detailed density) and the running sessions cell. Since 2026-09-28 (Joe), EVERY density, compact included, also draws a small icon-only scheduled-tasks marker beside the status light while at least one timer is live: no visible count or countdown, its hover title carries the same count-and-next-fire wording the clock chip's own tooltip does. Clicking the chip opens a read-only list: each timer's status (live, fired, canceled, replaced, expired, lost), its schedule, when it fires, and a redacted summary of its prompt, plus the watcher's count of open background shells and monitors. Since issue #945's follow-up (#1039), when a SUB-AGENT is what parked on its own open shell or Monitor - the case that used to show a session as working_subagent with nothing on screen explaining why - the list also names each one: which sub-agent, its task, its kind and how long it has been open, in one already-redacted sentence with no command or output ever shown. The same sentence appears in the status light's tooltip when that is the reason the light reads working_subagent. Nothing here feeds the light's colour or the auto-sleep idle clock.
examples: A session polling a CI run every 15 minutes shows a chip reading 12m, so you know when it will next report without opening it.
After a reboot the chip is gone and the list says lost, which tells you the loop needs starting again.
how_to: Have a claude session schedule itself, for example with /loop or by asking it to check back later, or to run something every 15 minutes.
Watch the icon-only marker and, at cozy/detailed, the clock chip appear beside that session within one watcher cycle.
Hover the marker, or read the chip, for the time to its next fire.
Click the chip to open the read-only list of every timer the conversation set, live ones first.
Restart the session: its timers were held by the old process, so the marker and chip go away and the list marks them lost.

catalog.description: An agent can bring a left bar item into view for you. The tool sidebar_show takes a kind (session, file, browser, board, layout or task_manager) and an id, checks the item exists, and shows it in the window you used last, the one with your latest click or key press. Your other windows and devices do not move. files_open and browser_open take an optional front flag that does the same for the row they just opened; it is off unless the agent sets it. If you have not used any window since the app started, or every window has closed, there is nothing to show it in, and the agent is told so. A window you close is forgotten, so the show falls back to the window you used before it. In the desktop app the window that gets the item also comes to the front.
examples: An agent opens plan.md with front true: the files row appears and the file fills the main section in the window you were just typing in, while your phone stays where it was.
An agent calls sidebar_show with kind layout and a layout's uuid: that layout opens in your current window.
An agent calls sidebar_show with kind task_manager: the Task Manager widget comes up in the window you used last.
You close the window you were typing in; an agent calls sidebar_show and the item opens in the window you used before it, and the desktop app brings that window to the front.
how_to: Nothing to turn on: use any window and agents can show things in it.
An agent calls the MCP tool sidebar_show with kind and id (no id for task_manager), or sets front true on files_open or browser_open.

POST /api/v1/ui/show {kind, id, target_client_id?} does the same (the optional target names one open window) over the API; POST /api/v1/ui/activity {client_id} is how a window reports that you used it, and POST /api/v1/ui/activity/gone how it reports that it closed.
Close a window and the next show goes to the window you used before it; in the desktop app the window that shows the item is raised, even from behind other apps.

catalog.description: Skill scout, in a session's session skills panel, pastes a short request into the running Claude agent. The request lists the skills of the signed catalog you have not installed (id, name, description; nothing unsigned) and a small digest of this conversation's own history: the skills it used most, the tools that keep failing and its last few corrections, with anything that looks like a credential dropped. It is refused, and nothing is pasted, when the pane is stopped on a question, dead or not an agent. The agent answers with lines of the form CARNIVORE-SKILL id | reason; the app reads them from the transcript and shows only ids that exist in the verified catalog, without duplicates and at most ten, each as a chip with the reason as plain text. A chip adds the skill to this project through the normal install path: one tap when the server allows it, the consent sheet otherwise; consent is never skipped.

catalog.description: The skills manager page lists every skill folder the app can find for one place: global (the default Claude profile and the Codex config), another Claude profile group (a profile with a real skills folder of its own says so), or one of your projects. Each skill has an on or off switch. In the detail pane a Claude skill also offers compact (the model sees only its name) and on demand (only you can run it), and a Codex skill offers on and off only, with a reminder that a running Codex session needs a restart. A plugin's skill has no switch because it switches with the whole plugin. Changes are written by the server to the right settings file: the global choice to the profile's settings.json (profile links stay links), a project choice to that project's .claude/settings.local.json. Locations can be removed (moved to a trash folder, never deleted); one installed from the catalog is removed there so its install record stays right. Chips narrow the list to claude, codex, off, shadowed and heavy skills, where heavy is an estimated per-turn cost of the description. Opening session skills from a terminal's menu shows the skills that pane's agent really has, a switch for each that writes that project's local settings, and its recent skill use. One tab sits beside the list. Census shows every skill in every root with how often it fired in the last 7, 30 and 90 days and its estimated per-turn cost (a skill nothing has measured says not measured, never 0), sortable by any column. Its two columns are separate panels with banded rows. Opening a skill shows all of its state in five sections: where it lives and its state per harness, usage and cost (fires in the last 7, 30 and 90 days, and the estimated per-turn cost), health (whether Sentinel says the installed copy was edited, with restore and keep as fork, Tripwire's verdict, and the autopsy of what followed its fires), provenance and trust (the install record, the signer, the security review, the digest and any deprecated note), and contents (the SKILL.md of each copy and the signed file list). The list marks a drifted, flagged or unused-for-30-days skill so problems stand out without opening each one; anything not measured says so instead of showing 0 or clean. With a text model chosen for skill card summaries in Settings > AI, each skill's card shows a one sentence summary that fits its three lines, written once per skill text and again only when the skill changes; with none chosen the card shows the plain description.

catalog.description: The session listing carries running and total subagent counts, measured by the attention watcher once per cycle and never collapsed from "not measured" or "not applicable" (codex) into zero. In the agents drawer the presentation depends on the row's density: cozy shows a clickable chip beside the status light, detailed shows a plain green count beside the agent icon instead, and every other density shows neither. Since 2026-09-28 (Joe), EVERY density, compact included, also draws a small icon-only marker beside the status light while a subagent is running or a background shell/monitor is parked (replacing the plain square badge issue #1039's follow-up had added): no visible count, its hover title carries the count and the parked reason. The running sessions cell always shows its own chip. Drawer headings and the running sessions header show sums, at every density. Clicking a chip opens a read-only list of the session's subagents: status, type, description and age. A subagent's activity also moves its parent session's last-worked time forward (never backward), so a session whose subagents are busy stays bold and near the top of the drawer and project ordering. The opscenter home dashboard has a SUBAGENTS stat tile (its own tile since the stat strip split, #1157) that shows the total running-subagent count across every live session, summed only from sessions the watcher actually measured, with the number of sessions it covers under it; a session that was never measured, or that cannot run subagents (codex), contributes nothing to that total, and the tile shows nothing rather than a fake zero when no session has been measured yet.

catalog.description: The board tab on the Swarm page shows every Swarm card in five views behind one switcher: swimlanes, list, timeline, calendar and columns by project. Swimlanes is the default. Swimlanes draws one lane per project (or named list) with a full-width header: the project name, its company, its card total, how many are done, the faces of the agents working its cards and a stacked bar of todo, in progress, review and done. An open lane shows its todo, in progress, review and done cards side by side in faintly tinted columns, five per cell with a +N more key; a card shows its number, age, title, a one-line summary of what it is for, who holds it, a working, queued, paused or stalled chip and its reported progress as a calm green bar. Click a card to open the same detail pane the list view uses. Drag a card to reorder its queue (the order agents are dealt cards) or into another column: in progress to todo pauses it, into done completes it. Each card carries quick action keys for its stage: top and bottom, pause, mark done, auto-promote for a todo card, reclassify with a note for the next agent, archive (the archived key brings it back), collapse to one line and delete with a confirm. Agents hear about a move about 15 seconds after the last change, so a quick undo never reaches them. A lane with nothing in progress or in review is folded to one line with its four counts, and your own fold or unfold is remembered on this device. Filter by scope (sysop, a company or a project), all cards or only yours, and search by #number or title. The board updates by itself when any card changes, and the device remembers the view you picked. The list view puts every card not yet done in three bands, the cards waiting on your review first under needs you, then in progress, then todo, each child right under its parent. Click a row to open its detail pane: the created, started, review and done steps with their times, its progress, result and how to validate it, its history newest first, and done or send back with a note, which mark the card through the same routes as everywhere else. The calendar view shows the week (or today, or the last three days) as a grid: one row per project grouped by company, and in each day how many of its cards were created, started, sent to review, approved or sent back, an hourly activity bar under it, the faces of the agents whose card started that day, a now line in today, hatched days still to come and a key at the bottom. The timeline view draws the last twelve hours (or three days, or a week) on a time scale: per project, each parent card as a thick bar with its children nested under it and a dashed link where each child reached review, then the cards with no parent. A bar shows waiting, working and review spans, grey where the start was never recorded; the working agent's face sits on every bar being worked and on its parent's line, a now line crosses every lane and the shared key sits at the bottom. The columns by project view puts each project in its own column with its cards stacked under its name, the ones waiting on your review first, then in progress, todo and done, five of each before a +N more key; each card carries its state glyph, the same quick action keys and opens the same detail pane, and a todo or queued card drags to a new place in its queue.
examples: see at a glance which projects have work in progress and which are idle
find a card by its number from any project
check how far along a working agent says it is
go through every card waiting on your review and mark it done or send it back with a note
see what each project got done today and this week in the calendar
see which parent cards moved in the last twelve hours and which agent is on each child
talk to a project's agent from its lane without leaving the board
see each project's work side by side, one column per project

catalog.description: The first slice of the swarm cards work. A card is a huddle task: nothing is copied and no task row is rewritten. Its board column is worked out from its state, who holds it, whether claude is working it and whether the agent that made it accepted the report: todo, in progress, review or done. The huddle database gains the card columns and tables in one migration that writes no rows, and the server takes a checked copy of the database (huddle.db.pre-cards plus the time) before it runs. One writer in the huddle plugin owns every card change, and a test fails if any other file writes a card column. A new cards push topic tells open browsers to re-read the board. This slice is backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.
examples: Open the board for one project and see which tasks are todo, which an agent holds in progress and which wait in review for your click.
