Add filter=mine to see only the cards you made; agent-made child cards fold under their parent.
Call GET /api/v1/swarm/cards/{card_id} for one card with its column, holder, children and origin.
catalog.media_exempt: backend only; the board UI waits for the layout pick
catalog.name: swarm cards: the card model and board reads
catalog.summary: every huddle task now reads as a card with one of four board columns (todo, in progress, review, done), readable through two new routes.
where: Backend only for now: read the board at GET /api/v1/swarm/cards/board with a scope (sysop, a company or a project), and one card at GET /api/v1/swarm/cards/{card_id}. The board screen arrives in a later slice.

catalog.description: The second slice of the swarm cards work. Swarm agents now work from cards: they start a card they were dealt, keep its handoff note current as a heartbeat, and finish it with a result and the steps to validate it, which puts it in Review. Only you move a card to Done, from the owner routes; no agent tool can. Spawning an agent gives it a card (the one you name, or one made from its goal). A card holder's report goes through the same finish path and is tied to the card, so accepting the report accepts the card; when the last child card of a parent is accepted the parent moves to Review with every child's steps merged. The owner routes add Done (which also approves the accepted children), send back with a note (the last holder gets the card again, and the note becomes a fact the project agent keeps), release, move, pause and resume with the cascade down child cards, swap, pin, and the per-project switches. This slice is backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.
examples: Send a card in Review back with the note 'use the new session api': the agent that finished it holds it again, gets your note word for word, and the project agent keeps the note as a fact with a learned line in its chat.

Pause a parent card with now: the agent holding it and every agent holding a child card are stopped and told to write their handoff, and the response lists the child cards and agents the pause reached.
how_to: Call POST /api/v1/swarm/cards/{card_id}/done on a card in Review to move it to Done as the owner.
Call POST /api/v1/swarm/cards/{card_id}/send-back with a note to reopen a Review card; the last holder is re-held when still alive, else the card waits in Todo.
Call PUT /api/v1/swarm/cards/rules/{project_id} with auto_done, reorder (suggest or auto), pace or dealing to change a project's switches.

Agents use the swarm_card_* tools: swarm_card_start, swarm_card_handoff, swarm_card_finish (result plus how_to_validate), swarm_card_release, swarm_card_create, swarm_card_reorder and swarm_card_deal.
catalog.media_exempt: backend only; the board UI waits for the layout pick
catalog.name: swarm cards: card tools and owner routes
catalog.summary: swarm agents start, hand off and finish cards through new tools, finishing puts a card in Review and only the owner routes move it to Done; spawn, reports, roll-up, send-back and pause are tied to cards.
where: Backend only for now: the owner routes live under /api/v1/swarm/cards and agents reach the same operations through the swarm_card_* tools. The board screen arrives in a later slice.

catalog.description: The third slice of the swarm cards work: dealing and leases. When cards enter a project's Todo queue, the server sends the project agent one deal request after a 5 second window, however many cards arrived, and wakes it if it sleeps. The request lists the top of the queue and the free agents, and stays open until the agent deals a card or answers with hold; an unanswered request is sent again after 15 minutes, three times in all, then a line in the chat tells you. Dealing is off for every project that existed when this shipped: turn it on per project with the dealing switch (a project made later starts on). A card an agent holds in progress carries a lease: 10 minutes with no card write, no busy reading and no stop reading hands it back for a new deal (the old agent is told to stop and the next agent starts from the handoff note), or, with dealing off, marks it stalled with one line in the chat. An open question, a permission or dialog on screen, or a pause stops the clock; a plain session's working claim never lapses. A working agent whose handoff note is half an hour old is asked once to refresh it. This slice is backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.
examples: Add five cards to a project's queue in a burst with dealing on: the project agent gets one deal request that lists all five, not five requests.

A card held by an agent that has shown no sign of life for ten minutes goes back to Todo marked handed off, and the project agent is asked to deal it again; with dealing off it stays with the agent, marked stalled, and the chat says it is waiting for you.
how_to: Call PUT /api/v1/swarm/cards/rules/{project_id} with dealing true to let the server deal that project's queue, false to stop it.
A project agent answers an open deal request with swarm_card_deal (a card and an agent) or with hold when nothing should start.
catalog.media_exempt: backend only; the board UI waits for the layout pick
catalog.name: swarm cards: dealing and leases
catalog.summary: new cards reach the project agent as one deal request, held cards lapse to a hand-off or a stalled line after ten quiet minutes, and dealing lands off for every existing project until you turn it on.
where: Backend only for now: the dealing switch is on the owner routes under /api/v1/swarm/cards/rules, and the deal request and lapse lines appear in the project agent's chat. The board screen arrives in a later slice.

catalog.description: The fourth slice of the swarm cards work: the capacity governor. A card dealt to an agent that has no body yet (asleep) needs a new body, and the governor decides whether that may start now. It waits when the project has no free slot (a project or company with no grant has no limit of its own since #1439, and you or SysOp can grant 0 to 20 per project or company; while a project is throttled for merge conflicts it runs at most 3), or when the machine is hot: the CPU has been over 85 percent for the last two minutes, or a fresh usage window is over 90 percent on the Claude account the new agent will run on (a different account that is parked at its limit holds nothing back; when that account cannot be told, every account counts). The capacity reading, the slot refusal, the spawn refusal and the deal request name that account and the window that tripped. A deal that waits shows the card marked waiting for a slot, and the server deals it by itself, oldest first, once a slot frees. The governor never pauses, sleeps or kills running work, never touches a card an agent already holds, and a deal to an awake agent always goes through. The governor's CPU reading is whole-machine busy time; separately, since #1439 every new agent body is admitted by measuring the machine (load average per core and free memory), and refused with system is pegged, try later and a retry_after when it cannot take one. While a project's dealing switch is off the two machine floors do not apply, so your own explicit deals are not held back by a hot machine. SysOp and company agents read the numbers with swarm_card_capacity, set grants with swarm_card_grant and set a project's pace (normal: one card per free agent, asap: use every free slot) with swarm_card_pace; the deal request the project agent receives now names its free slots, the cards waiting for one and the pace. This slice is backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.
examples: Grant a project 2 slots while two of its agents are running: a card dealt to a third, sleeping agent reads waiting for a slot, and starts by itself the moment one of the two finishes.
With the CPU over 85 percent for two minutes and dealing on, a deal to a sleeping agent waits; the agents already working are not touched, and the card is dealt when the machine cools.
how_to: Call GET /api/v1/swarm/cards/capacity for the CPU busy figure, the highest usage window on the account new agents run on (usage_account, usage_window), live agents against the caps and whether a floor is on.
Call PUT /api/v1/swarm/cards/grants/project:16 with slots 0 to 20 and a reason to cap a project (company:3 for a company); send slots null to go back to the default.
catalog.media_exempt: backend only; the board UI waits for the layout pick
catalog.name: swarm cards: capacity governor
catalog.summary: a deal that needs a new agent waits for a slot when the grant is full or the machine is hot, and is dealt by itself when one frees; grants and pace come from SysOp, company agents and you.
where: Backend only for now: the owner routes under /api/v1/swarm/cards (capacity, grants), the swarm_card_capacity, swarm_card_grant and swarm_card_pace tools for SysOp and company agents, and the slots and pace lines in a project agent's deal request. The board screen arrives in a later slice.

catalog.description: The agent side of swarm cards. A feature or task agent's brief now teaches the card loop: start the card, keep the handoff current, finish with a result and how-to-validate steps, release when stuck, and never mark a card done. A project agent's standing rules add how to run the queue: deal the top cards in order, hold when nothing should start, split big cards, accept or reject reports and suggest reorders. Every wake, fresh or resumed, repeats a short card duty. A dealt card's message lists up to three facts its chain already knows, with their ids, so what a parent learned travels down, and a spawned child's first message lists them next to its card. The huddle guide moves to revision 6 and teaches plain sessions the four columns, that a swarm-held card refuses huddle state writes, and that only you reach Done. Backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.
examples: Spawn a task agent and read its brief: section 4 tells it to start its card, write a handoff as it goes and finish with how to validate.
Deal a card to an agent whose parent remembered a related fact: the deal message names that fact with its f_ id.
Spawn a task agent whose parent remembered a related fact: the child's first message names that fact with its f_ id.
how_to: Read a project agent's creation brief or its next wake to see the dealing rules after its delegation sentence.
Call huddle_guide and check guide_rev is 6; section 18 is the cards section.
Kill a fact you do not want passed down with DELETE /api/v1/swarm/facts/{fact_id}.
catalog.media_exempt: backend only; the board UI waits for the layout pick
catalog.name: swarm cards: agent rules and learning down
catalog.summary: swarm agents are taught the card loop in their briefs and on every wake, project agents get the dealing rules, a dealt card carries the facts its chain already knows, and the huddle guide moves to rev 6.
where: Backend only for now: the rules reach agents through their briefs, wake texts and the huddle guide. The board screen arrives in a later slice.

catalog.description: The sixth slice of the swarm cards work. Every line in an agent's conversation now carries a category (conversation, result, question, important, dealt, and so on), and card traffic lines that carry one now show in the conversation instead of being dropped. A new swarm_chat_muted preference hides categories: the conversation route takes view=shown to drop what you muted (unset shows only conversation, result, question and important), while view=all, the default, drops nothing. Your own words and the agent's can never be muted. The only thing that goes to your phone is a question that climbed to you because no agent above the asker could answer it: it is one push of its own type, swarm.question_climbed, seeded on web push and native app push only, and the question card is marked sent to your phone only when a destination actually took the push (a type left unticked, quiet hours or paused routing leave it unmarked). A swarm body's own finished, attention and posted toasts stay in the app (matched on the body's own tmux instance, so a later plain session that reuses a destroyed body's name still pushes); its permission, question and plan dialogs still go out. This slice is backend only: the chat filter UI waits for the layout pick. The chat's "waiting on me" and an agent's node read one server answer (#2595): only a question still open whose asker has not been torn down or woken again since asking waits on you; a card in Review never does, and a failed-wake or dead-body card about a torn-down agent raises no alert. Stale ones are closed with a record, never deleted.
examples: Mute dealt and handed_off lines with swarm_chat_muted, then read an agent's conversation with view=shown: those lines are gone and your own messages stay.

An agent asks something no one above it can answer: your web push destination gets one swarm question for you push once you tick that type on the notifications screen, and the card reads sent to your phone; with that type unticked everywhere the card stays unmarked.
how_to: Call GET /api/v1/swarm/agents/{id}/conversation?view=shown to read a conversation without the categories you muted; view=all returns everything, each entry with its category.
PATCH /api/v1/preferences with swarm_chat_muted set to a list of category names to choose what hides; leave it unset for the default of conversation, result, question and important only.
Tick swarm question for you on a destination in the notifications screen to get the climbed-question push there (an existing destination starts with it off).
catalog.media_exempt: backend only; the board UI waits for the layout pick
catalog.name: swarm chat categories, mute and phone
catalog.summary: swarm conversations carry a category per line with a mute preference and a shown view, and only a question that climbed to you pushes to your phone.
where: Backend only for now: read a conversation at GET /api/v1/swarm/agents/{id}/conversation (view=all or view=shown), set the mute list through the swarm_chat_muted preference, and tick the swarm question for you type on the notifications screen. The chat filter screen arrives with the board UI.

catalog.description: The seventh slice of the swarm cards work. A card in Review can now be validated: the project agent starts a fresh task agent that runs the card's how-to-validate steps (through a validator agent definition when the project has one, else with its own tools) and ends with a pass or fail verdict plus the proof it saw, kept word for word on the card. A pass marks the card validated and, when the project's auto-done switch is on, moves it to Done, after re-checking inside the Done write that the pass still covers the card (a send-back and re-finish, or a newer validation run, in between keeps it in Review). A fail sends the card back to In Progress marked validation failed with the proof, held again by the agent that finished it, which is told what failed. With nothing to validate it, the card reads no proof yet and the validate route answers 409. You start a validation from the validate route, or turn on the project's auto-validate switch so every card that reaches Review is validated by itself. This slice is backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.
examples: A card is finished with the steps 'run pytest -q and open the page'. Validate it: a task agent runs both, reports 'ran pytest -q: 3 failed' as a fail, and the card goes back to the agent that built it, marked validation failed, with that text as the proof.
With auto-validate and auto-done both on for a project, a card that reaches Review is validated; on a pass it moves to Done by itself, and on a fail it goes back to In Progress.
how_to: Call POST /api/v1/swarm/cards/{card_id}/validate on a card in Review to start a validation now; it answers 409 no_capability when the project has no validator agent and no project agent.
Call GET /api/v1/swarm/cards/{card_id}/validation to read the state, the proof (null reads no proof yet), what would validate the card and whether a start would be accepted.
Call PUT /api/v1/swarm/cards/rules/{project_id} with auto_validate to validate every card that reaches Review, and auto_done to finish a card after a pass.
The validating agent ends with the swarm_card_verdict tool: card_id, verdict pass or fail, and the proof.
catalog.media_exempt: backend only; the board UI waits for the layout pick
catalog.name: swarm cards: validation
catalog.summary: a card in Review can be validated by a fresh task agent (or a validator agent definition) that returns pass or fail with its proof; a fail sends the card back marked validation failed, a pass can finish it.
where: Backend only for now: the owner routes live under /api/v1/swarm/cards (validate and validation) and the validating agent uses the swarm_card_verdict tool. The board screen arrives in a later slice.

catalog.description: The eighth slice of the swarm cards work. A company agent (or SysOp) can now make one parent card in its own list and hang child cards on it in several of its projects' queues; each child is dealt by that project's own project agent, as any card is. Children of another company's project are refused, and a company agent adds children only under its own cards or its company's project cards. When every child, in any project, is done, the parent moves to Review by itself with a merged how-to-validate (n of n done, plus each child's steps and proof), and your Done on the parent finishes the children too. On the company and SysOp board a parent shows once in its own lane and again in the lane of every project that holds one of its children, marked as the parent of the cards in that lane. This slice is backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.
examples: A company agent makes the card 'launch the new line' and a child in project Zeta and another in project Alpha. Zeta's agent and Alpha's agent each deal their own child. When both are accepted the parent reads Review, 2 of 2 done, and shows in both project lanes on the company board.
Company 2's agent tries to hang a child in its own project under company 1's card and is refused; Alpha (SysOp) may do it anywhere.
how_to: Make the parent in the company agent's own list, then make each child with the swarm_card_create tool naming the parent and the project_id of the project it goes in.
Read GET /api/v1/swarm/cards/board?scope=company:<id> or scope=sysop; a cross-project parent has lane_role parent_of_children_here in every lane but its own.
Click Done on the parent in Review (POST /api/v1/swarm/cards/{id}/done) to finish it and its children.
catalog.media_exempt: backend only; the board UI waits for the layout pick
catalog.name: swarm cards: cross-project cards
catalog.summary: a company or SysOp card can have children in several projects' queues, each dealt by its own project agent; the parent rolls up to Review across projects and shows in every child's lane at company scope.
where: Backend only for now: the company and SysOp board at /api/v1/swarm/cards/board and the swarm_card_create tool. The board screen arrives in a later slice.

catalog.description: A widget for the right widget bar (the bar the notepad lives on). Its key opens a drawer beside the terminal, sized like the notepad: drag the drawer's left edge for width and, when it shares the drawer with another widget, drag the line between them for height. One item per row, never nested, in the order questions, reviews, working, waiting, scheduled, open, the item touched last first inside a status. A row is the Task Manager's own status mark, the title and how old it is; a question wears a yellow stripe. Compact rows are one 20px line so eight or more fit; two-line rows add the latest message under the title with who wrote it. The title row carries the count and the two density keys, which show when the pointer or focus is in the row. Hover a title or second line that is cut off with an ellipsis to see all of it. Press a row to open it in place, one at a time: a question shows the Task Manager's real answer form, a review its latest line and the reply box, every other row its latest line, and each has open in task manager. Right-click the widget's key, or anywhere in the list, for the six status checks of the Task Manager's badge menu under the heading show in list; ticking keeps the menu open and the ticks are stored on that copy, so you can place it more than once with different statuses, and they sync to every device. The key's badge is the number of rows the copy lists. The list is pushed from the Task Manager's own store and never polls.
examples: Keep only questions and reviews ticked for a short list of what waits on you.
Add a second copy with only working ticked to watch what the agents are doing.
how_to: Open edit layout and drag the Task Manager list widget from the widgets drawer onto the right widget bar.
Press its key to open the drawer; drag the drawer's left edge to size it.
Right-click the key (or the list) and tick the statuses you want to see; the menu stays open.
Press a row to open it in place; a question shows the answer form.
Use the two icons in the title row to switch between compact and two-line rows.
Use the status and folder icons in the title row to group the rows under headers by status or by project; each header shows its count.

Press open in task manager on an open row: the Task Manager widget comes up (its bar opens if it was shut), the group unfolds and the task scrolls into view. With no Task Manager widget placed, a small warning says to add one from edit layout.
catalog.media_exempt: A widget whose screenshots are captured before the next version bump.
catalog.name: Task Manager list widget
catalog.summary: The Task Manager's items in one flat list on the right widget bar, beside the notepad: questions first, then reviews, working, waiting, scheduled and open, with a count, and you tick which statuses show from the right-click menu. Off until you add it.
where: The right widget bar, once added: a key with the list icon and a count badge.

catalog.description: A two-way list you and claude both write to, in a tab of the left sidebar. There is one list per project and one shared all projects list. Claude adds items (done: this, need your call: that), marks them done and asks you a question on any item; you add items for claude, drag them into priority order, check the ones that are good, and leave a note where it is good but claude should read something. A checked item with a note reads good, read the note. Each item has a short thread: claude asks, you reply, and your reply answers its question. When claude posts, a notice fires and the tab's badge turns yellow while a question waits, without taking you away from the tab you are on; the tab sits in the strip while the show tab setting is on and has no close key. Tell carnivore in the tab's title row sends one line to a claude session of the project saying the list changed, picking the most recently active one or letting you choose. Claude reads only what changed through its task manager tools and can never approve, reorder or delete. The pop out key in the title row opens the task manager in its own window so it sits beside what you are working on.
examples: Claude finishes a change and adds done: the folder picker; you check it, and claude sees it is approved the next time it reads the list.
You add fix the toast colour to the project's list, drag it to the top and press tell carnivore.
Claude asks which of two names you want on an item; the swarm tab shows a yellow badge, you reply in the thread.
You ask claude what it needs from you right now; it highlights the two items waiting on your call and opens the most urgent one, in the sidebar and the pop-out alike, until you touch the list.
Claude replies on an item while you are away; when you come back the row wears the unread light and the tab badge says 1; opening the row clears it on your phone too.

While claude works on your item it adds a note on the thread: the row keeps its working stripe, shows no unread dot and gets a small yellow light until you open it; when claude wants you to look at a result the row's light turns blue and counts as unread.
Claude marks an item done and it moves into ready to review; you write a reply on it and it moves out of ready to review into open, then to working once claude reads it.
You screenshot a broken layout, paste it into the reply box and press reply; claude reads the picture from its path on the thread.
Claude flags three items purple with the reason needs a decision; you see the purple stripes and one legend entry, and the flags clear as you tick each item.
Claude asks to rename the project 'api' to 'api-v2' for item 215; the row moves to needs you and says so, you press approve, the project is renamed and claude is told the result.

You switch the nudge on for a project (the edit project modal or the bell on its bar); an open item goes quiet for an hour, carnivore wakes that project's idle agent about it, and after three nudges with no change the item asks you to unstick it.
You reply on a task, press tell, and see sent to carnivore 14:31 then reply received 14:31 under your message; ten minutes later a bell on another task's row shows the agent never fetched your reply.
how_to: The task manager is called swarm in the app. It ships on for a clean install and stays off on an existing install until you turn it on: open the plugins page from the menu tab, find swarm (marked plugin) and press its switch, which grants what it asks.

Open the menu tab and choose swarm: the plugins page opens on the swarm plugin's side pane, at its settings (link: #plugins/huddle/settings). The show tab switch (on by default) keeps the swarm tab in the strip with no close key; switch it off to hide the tab, on any browser. The swarm look and page fields are in the same section, below the switches.
Pick a list at the top: all projects or one project.
Type in the box at the bottom and press add to give claude an item.
Drag a row by its dotted grip to change its priority, or focus the grip and press the up and down arrows.
Check a row to approve it; press the note key to add a note, which makes it good, read the note.
Click a row (or press Enter on it) to open it: the thread sits under the description, with claude's question and your reply box. A question or review row also carries its own reply box.
Paste a picture or file into a reply box, or drop files on it: each uploads at once and shows as a chip (the x removes it); send posts them with your words, or alone.

Press tell carnivore at the bottom right to tell a claude session the list changed now; your ordinary changes also go out on their own a few seconds after you stop. If the list has no session, a pop-up above the key offers start a new session, a running session, or stop.
Press the pop out key in the title row to open the task manager in its own window.
Press hide completed (the eye, icon only) in the bar to hide checked items (it stays off until you turn it on, on every device); the eye shows whether it is on, and unchecking an item brings it back.

Press the count at the far left of the bar (the number of checked items), then the red delete key, to delete the checked items of the list on screen; the confirm says they are gone for good, not hidden.
Press the lines key beside the add box to type several items at once, one per line.

Ask claude what it needs from you: it marks those tasks with one of eight solid shapes (the marker), which sit in the row's left margin; the list bar then shows a key for each shape in use, and pressing one shows only those tasks with every project and group opened.
Press the magnifier in the list bar to search tasks loosely ('rvwbrd' finds 'review board'); everything opens while you search and only matching tasks show; the clear key brings your folds back.

On a project header, press the info badge to read that project's infos in a list and dismiss them, press any other status badge to show only that status everywhere (press it again to clear), and click the project's name to fold or unfold it.

When claude wants a ticked item reopened, or an open one closed, it asks with a reason: the request waits in the approvals inbox as one card (title, current and target state, reason), nothing changes until you approve, and the answer is left as a line on the item. Closing means your approve is the tick.

The keys at the foot are icons only, with their names on hover: far left the remove completed count, then (in the by group view only) new group and show empty groups, and on the right hide completed (the eye) and tell carnivore (the arrow). The add box sits in its own strip below them.

A row with the green unread light holds something claude added, changed, answered or pointed at since you last looked; open or tick it to clear the light on every device. The tab badge and the list picker count the unread rows.

Read a row's left stripe for who it waits on: bright yellow is claude's question for you, green is claude working on it, cyan is claude done and waiting on your review, violet is built but not yet installed; hover the row number for the words.

Tell carnivore tells every changed list into its own session (from all projects, each list that changed); a list with no session to tell comes up in one pop-up where you pick a session for it. The number inside tell carnivore counts your changes not yet sent, and drops to 0 as soon as a tell sends them.

Each row shows a small status icon at its left (question, working, ready to review, waiting to install, ticked, open, todo); an info icon there means claude left a message you have not opened yet. An item with a change claude has not read yet shows as open.
Open an item to read its thread as a chat under the description: claude on the left, you on the right, in its own scroll box that opens on the newest message.
By group, each group splits into status subsections (for example, widgets: question for you); done and todo start folded.

Hide a status you do not want to see: on the list bar's right end press the funnel to open the status filter card: one icon per status the list shows. All are on and the funnel is dim; click one to hide its rows in every view, click again to show them. Your choice is remembered on this device. With anything hidden the funnel turns blue. A hidden status that still holds items waiting on you (needs you, question, ready to review) shows a red ! on its key and on the funnel.
The add box's list follows the project of the tab you are on, while the list on screen stays where you put it.

Press the folder key at the left of the control row to make a named group in the list on screen; drag a row by its grip onto a group (or its header when folded) to file it there, and back above the groups to ungroup it.
A group's header folds it (every device folds together); hover it for rename, up, down and remove. Removing a group keeps its items, ungrouped. An open item's move to key also lists the groups.
Ask claude to sort the list into groups: it makes them and files items with task_manager_group_create and the group argument of task_manager_add and task_manager_move.

Press enter in a reply box or the one-line add box to save it; the tell about that list is queued and goes out after a few quiet seconds, or when you press tell carnivore (in the multiline box enter is a new line and cmd+enter adds).

The list sorts itself by status (the default): needs you, question for you, ready to review, waiting to install, working, scheduled, open, todo and done (todo and done start folded); items move between them on their own. Each row wears its area as a small tag. Press by group at the top to see your groups instead and drag between them; the choice holds on every device.

When claude asks typed questions (yes or no, pick one, pick many, rank, short or long text) the row shows one line, N questions, with an answer key. It opens a form with claude's recommendations marked: take one with its take recommendation key, or take all recommendations, add a note to any answer, and submit. Submit saves the answer and queues the tell like any other change. A plain reply on a typed ask is a comment: it does not answer the form.

In the swarm panel click an agent: its chat opens in a drawer on the right at the left drawer's width. Drag the drawer's left edge to resize it (the width is remembered on this device), press escape or the close key to shut it, or click another agent to swap it. The tasks viewer tab shows the task manager list of that one agent. A reply, add or tick is sent when you submit it: there is no send queue, and a tell to a busy agent shows as held until it is free.

Send something to the Task Manager and the browser keeps a copy until the server takes it: if the server hiccups the copy is sent again on its own, and the developer widget's sent tab can copy it or download all of them. A task with subtasks (its forks) cannot be ticked until every subtask is done, and a task that still waits on its forks cannot be ticked at all: the tick stays empty and the list says why, naming each subtask and what it waits on. catalog.description: Right of the usage meters in the terminal's bottom bar, a segment shows the running subagents and the open background shells and monitors (agents 2 bg 1), and a clock shows the live timer count and the time to the next fire. The server only stops a process that is still the same process it listed and sits under that session's own agent: never the agent, never the pane's shell, never anything outside the session. catalog.description: Plugins installed from the catalog run as isolated processes in a macOS sandbox, never inside the app. Nothing third-party runs until you turn the master switch on, and turning it off stops every one of them. The switch shows whether the sandbox is ready on this computer; where it is not (a Python without the framework build), plugins refuse to start and the page says why. Safe mode stops them all at once without removing anything. A plugin you install starts off with no permissions and asks again when its code changes.

examples: You remove a session and later find its transcript file is gone; restore the point from the session's conversation backups tab and resume the same conversation.
how_to: Turn on conversation backups (the save plugin) in plugins. It ships off; an install that already had it on keeps it on.

Conversation backups copy every conversation on disk into the backup vault when the plugin is turned on and keep it current as the conversation grows; killing, removing, sleeping or restarting a session also saves a point at that moment. A conversation whose file was later shortened or rewritten keeps the older point.
Open a session on the projects page and use its conversation backups tab, or GET /api/v1/cplugs/save/sessions/{session_uuid}/points; pin a point so it never ages out, or restore it.

A restore always puts the transcript back. Starting a session on it needs the permissions sessions.read and sessions.create, which you grant to the plugin on the plugins page; without them the tab tells you so in plain words.

Set how much disk conversation backups may use, and what they capture, in the plugin's settings pane on the plugins page (the storage slider and the capture scope: human, human and subsessions, or all; GET and PUT /api/v1/cplugs/save/settings and /capture-scope).

The vault never deletes a conversation's last copy, never deletes to get under the size limit, and tells you in the backup health alerts when it is over the limit, cannot be reached, has fallen behind, or holds conversations with no copy.

Choose where the vault lives in the plugin's settings pane (vault location, the setting vaultLocation; blank is the app data folder). A folder that is a symlink, inside iCloud, CloudStorage or Dropbox, or cannot be used now is refused and nothing is stored; a folder on the same disk as your transcripts is allowed with a warning. A new location starts a new vault; nothing is moved and the old folder stays.

Plugin folders marked for the vault (the review boards and their drafts first) are backed up hourly into the same vault, git history included. GET /api/v1/cplugs/save/folders lists them with their size; POST /api/v1/cplugs/save/folders/{unit}/restore puts a copy in a new folder beside the original and never touches the original.

Old archive databases, recovered transcripts and the retired save store come in through POST /api/v1/cplugs/save/imports/preview (counts and a fingerprint, writes nothing) and POST /imports/apply (add only; undo with POST /imports/{run_id}/undo); an imported point shows an imported chip and its labels in the restore points table, and a junk, trash or review labeled import stays out of deep search until the once-over records a keep verdict.

catalog.description: The time machine check plugin runs tmutil once every 15 minutes (first pass a minute after it starts), off the event loop, and keeps one alert. A backup older than 24 hours raises it at once; a read that fails raises a cannot-tell alert on the second pass in a row, with a check access explainer that opens the Full Disk Access setting; a backup running right now changes nothing; a healthy backup, or a computer with no Time Machine destination, closes the alert. Its re-check now button posts to the plugin's own route. It ships off for everyone and needs only the notify permission.
examples: A laptop away from its backup disk for two days gets the stale alert.
A new install without Full Disk Access gets the cannot-tell alert with the steps.

how_to: Open the plugins page and switch on the time machine check; macOS asks nothing, but reading the newest backup needs Full Disk Access for Carnivore, and the cannot-tell alert's check access button opens that setting.

catalog.description: task-manager-dev-tools is an experimental plugin of the dev tier: hidden and not loaded until you turn on developer mode (Settings, Advanced), and then off by default. It needs the task manager. It gives Claude three tools for your task manager screen. task_manager_dev_scroll_set scrolls the task manager to the top in every browser you have open (optionally switching to one project first). task_manager_dev_fold_set folds or unfolds a project (its bar, status sections and groups), a named group, or a task, and with action close collapses an opened task card back to its row without changing any task. task_manager_dev_tasks_list lists projects or tasks compactly (id, title, status, project, group, tag), filtered by any mix of project, status, group, tag and kind, so Claude can answer what the open questions are, what tasks are open, or what is open in one project. Scroll and fold are pushed to the browsers, which act on the task manager's own fold state; nothing is polled and nothing new is stored. With the plugin off there are no routes and no tools.
examples: Ask Claude what the open questions are and it lists the tasks whose status is question, with project and group.
Ask Claude to fold the carnivore project and its bar, status sections and groups fold on your screen.
Ask Claude to close the card you have open and it collapses back to its row.

Ask Claude to scroll to the top, fold or unfold a project or group, close the open card, or list tasks by status; it calls task_manager_dev_scroll_set, task_manager_dev_fold_set and task_manager_dev_tasks_list.

catalog.description: A full-screen terminal client for the computer's own Carnivore server. Ssh in, run carnivore tui, log in once with the authenticator code and drive your sessions from the keyboard: see every session with its status light, attach and detach, start, stop, restart (live restarts need an arm key first), mark read, answer approvals, and read the usage ledger and the catalog.
examples: Ssh into the computer, run carnivore tui, press 1 and move with j and k to a session marked as waiting, press enter to attach, answer in the pane, detach with the tmux prefix and d and land back on the list.
Press 2 on the approvals screen and press a to approve or d to deny a pending request without opening a browser.
Press ? on any screen to see every key, listed by screen.
Open Settings, Terminal, carnivore tui in the dev-mode app, press install command, approve the admin prompt, then ssh in and run carnivore tui.

With the server stopped, ssh in and run carnivore tui: it says the server did not answer and opens offline mode, lists the sessions from tmux marked server down: read from tmux, press w to watch one read only or t to type into it.
how_to: Open Settings, Terminal, carnivore tui and press install command if it says not installed; approve the admin prompt on the computer. Or run the shown command from a terminal.
On the computer, or over ssh, run carnivore tui (from a source checkout, run the checkout command shown in the same block).
Enter the six digit authenticator code once; later runs reuse the saved login.
Press 1 to 4 to switch screens and ? for the full key list.
When the server is down, carnivore tui opens offline mode by itself (or run carnivore tui --offline): w watches, t or enter types, f fits the pane to this window, a shows every session on the socket.

catalog.description: Admins signed in with a passkey review submissions by status. Opening a row shows the stored gate report, code files and sizes, AI summary and findings with scan coverage, and the diff against the published version. Approve quotes the report digest so you approve exactly what you saw. Reject and an AI-only override ask for a written reason; override covers skills, themes and both plugin runtimes. Missing scans and integrity failures cannot be overridden. The publish worker signs and publishes approved submissions; revoke takes a published item back.
examples: Review a plugin's code inventory and AI findings, then approve publication or reject with a reason.
Revoke a published item and the signed revocation reaches apps at their next index refresh.
how_to: Sign in with your passkey and open a status tab.
Open a row to read code inventory, AI findings and coverage, the gate report and diff; approve, reject or override an AI-only block with a reason.
Open a published row and press revoke with a reason to take it back.

catalog.description: A BBS-themed view of the Warez page. The first time you ever open Warez, or when you click the gray pi in the bottom-right corner of the Warez menu (tooltip ELITE ACCESS), it dials a pretend modem (real handshake sound, always on with no off switch, and text, 8.4 seconds, any key skips), draws the logo line by line and drops you at the board: a header with the node box, the last callers on this computer, the file counts and install total, and a main menu in one double frame. It reads the same signed catalog and this computer's install ledger as the Warez page, in a bitmap VGA face and one of two palettes (carnivore red or oblivion green) picked by the theme's accent. The file area lists every file in the index as numbered rows (name, kind, real install count, a two-line brief, no id line) with [upd!] and [inst] markers; every menu letter filters or sorts it, l lists the top ten by measured installs, / searches, and r redials the index (the cached listing stays on screen under a NO CARRIER banner while it is offline).
examples: Open Warez for the very first time: the modem dials, the logo draws and docks, and the main menu appears under the node box. Every later visit shows the normal Warez page.
Press any key during the dial-up to skip it, then press a menu letter to see it echoed at the main menu prompt.
Press g to hang up: NO CARRIER shows, any key dials again, Esc goes back to Warez.
Open /#elite/board to land on the board with no dial-up.
Press s for skills only, i for installed only, then d to sort by downloads; the counts on the FILES and STATE panels follow what you narrowed.
Press / and type a word, Enter lists the matches over every kind, Esc clears the search and shows everything again.
Press l for the top ten by measured install counts; a file whose count could not be read is left out, never shown as zero.
how_to: Open Warez from the menu: the first time ever you land in Elite Access. After that, click the gray pi in the bottom-right corner of the Warez menu (on a phone, the bottom-right of the menu screen).
Any key or click skips the dial-up. On a page opened without a click, the first key or click starts the sound.
Alt+D dials again, Alt+H hangs up, Esc returns to Warez.
Use /#elite for the dial-up and /#elite/board to go straight to the board.
In the board: a s t m p pick a kind, i v u n narrow by state, f w o e d c sort, l the top ten, / searches, : or the Command line takes a typed command, r redials the index.

Enter opens the FILE_ID.DIZ of the file under the bar (a sheet on a phone), Shift+= adds or updates it, = tries it, Shift+M comments, Alt+Up and Alt+Down scroll the pane, Shift+D downloads, Shift+U updates and Shift+C clears the tagged files, ? lists every key.

catalog.description: The war room is a page of its own, opened from the menu row, the c key in the menu or the link #warroom. Its wall shows one small read-only terminal per running session, grouped by project in the project colours, each with the session's status light and name. A tile connects only while it is on screen and repaints about once a second (four times a second under the pointer); hovering a tile scales it up and floats it over its neighbours without moving them, and a click opens the session. Four switches in the widget's header and menu add the extras, all remembered per browser: shells (off), browsers (off), asleep sessions (off, drawn as dimmed cards that wake the session when clicked) and paired computers (on, with an offline card while a link is down). The page is also the third one edit layout works on, after Home and the terminal page: drag any widget onto it beside the wall. The arrangement is saved on the server and is the same on every desktop. There is no war room on a phone: the menu row is hidden at 700 pixels wide and narrower.
examples: Open the war room on a second monitor and leave it there.
Turn on asleep, then click a dimmed card to wake that session.
Put the running sessions count and the providers widget beside the wall.
how_to: Open the drawer's menu tab and press the war room row, or press c while the menu has focus.
Hover a tile to enlarge it and refresh it faster; click it to open that session.

Drag the peek zoom slider in the widget header (or pick a stop in its menu) to set how big the hover peek is: the steps are equal from 0 (no zoom) to 100 (twice the default peek), the same peek width at every tile count. Resting tiles show the session's bottom rows filling the tile.
Use the shells, browsers, asleep and paired computers switches in the widget header (or its menu) to add or remove those tiles.
Press edit layout (right click on empty space, or the layout button) to open the widgets drawer on the war room.
Drag a widget, for example a stats tile, from the drawer onto the page; it is saved at once and kept after a reload.
Press reset in edit layout to put the page back to the wall alone.

catalog.description: Every widget this build carries, on the shared manager frame, as a places podium: a rail filters by group, by what fits a place and by state; a sticky podium of five places (right bar, bottom bar, drawer cards, glance row, dashboards) sits over the grouped widget cards, each with a live preview and marks for where it already is. A widget goes into a place by dragging its card onto the place, by the plus in the place's heading, or by the card's add button and its menu; a place can be picked to show only what fits it, and rows in a place reorder by drag or alt up and down and come out with remove, each with an undo toast. Switching a widget off takes it out of every place. A widget that is off is no longer offered in any widgets menu. Fits is advice drawn from the sizes a widget declares; nothing is refused. Widgets are built into the app, so the page says plainly that none can be installed or removed here.

catalog.description: Every configured launch wrapper on the shared manager frame, grouped by type (family), each group with a heading row that names the count and the type's default wrapper (or says there is none) and a plus that adds a wrapper of that type; each wrapper shows its family, the command it runs, the live sessions launched through it and its whole script. Add a wrapper for any family (claude, codex, hermes, openclaw, shell), scoped to whichever family chip is pressed; edit one's label, script, entry, description and model flag; make one the default for its family; and remove one, all from this page (settings-page-move, 2026-09-28 - this used to be split between this page, read only, and Settings, which owned the writes). A wrapper's family and id are fixed once it exists - the id is also a launched session's stored agent type, so moving a wrapper to a different family would change what an already-launched session resolves to; add a new wrapper in the family you want instead. Export saves a wrapper as a small JSON file to share; import checks a shared file, shows its whole script, and writes only after you tick that you read it. An imported wrapper is never made a default. Each wrapper can wear its own icon, chosen with the shared icon picker in its detail pane; the same icon marks it in the new session menu and the restart and wake picker, and its share file carries it. The frame's own actions share it: export in the detail pane saves the file, remove takes away a wrapper that is not a default and that no live session runs through, after asking, and install in the title strip opens the reviewed import.
examples: Send a teammate your claude-chrome wrapper so their sessions launch with the same browser tools.
Check which live sessions still run through an old wrapper before you delete it in settings.

changes.details: A pre-accept auth rejection on /ws/events made the browser fail the opening handshake, which a real browser can never turn into an observable 4401 close code - onopen never fires and the close event carries 1006. The reconnect loop only recognized a literal 4401, so it retried with the same stale access token every ~30s forever instead of refreshing it. It now treats a close that never reached onopen as an auth rejection, refreshes the token through the same single-flight path REST calls use, and reconnects; a dead refresh token surfaces the signed-out state instead of retrying forever.
changes.summary: fix the live event channel looping on a stale token forever instead of refreshing it

changes.details: The /ws/terminal and /ws/browser sockets share the same pre-accept auth close /ws/events had (issue #1055): a bad token makes the server refuse the opening handshake before accept(), so a real browser never sees the app's own 4401 code, only a plain close with no onopen. A close that never opens is not always an auth problem though - it also looks exactly like an ordinary dropped connection or a server that has not come back up, and guessing wrong broke an existing /ws/browser test. Both sockets now confirm via the same refresh every REST 401 already uses before treating an unopened close as a rejection: a rotated token reconnects at once, a genuine refusal is left to the app's own sign-out handling, and an inconclusive refresh (no network, no refresh token on hand) changes nothing about the existing backoff or outage recovery. The confirm-and-classify logic is shared in one new module per frontend tree (client/js/socket-auth-recovery.js, web/src/lib/socket-auth-recovery.ts), also adopted by the /ws/events fix from earlier the same day.
